(p-30) Surat Ibrahim (peace be upon him). It is Meccan, except for verses twenty-eight and twenty-nine, which are Medinan. Its number of verses is fifty-two.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra.﴾ The discussion of this has passed, and its place (in the commentary) has been mentioned more than once. God Most High says: ﴿A Book﴾. It is the predicate (khabar) of it, if "Alif. Lam. Ra." is the subject (mubtada'), or it is the predicate of an implied subject, if "Alif. Lam. Ra." is itself a predicate of an omitted subject. Or it is recited in the style of enumeration. It may also be a second predicate of this omitted subject. God Most High says: ﴿We have sent it down to you﴾, which is an attribute (sifah) of it. God Most High says: ﴿so that you may bring mankind﴾, which is connected with ﴿We have sent it down﴾. That is, so that you may bring them all out, by means of the clear proofs contained within it, which make manifest that it is from God, Mighty and Majestic, and which reveal the true beliefs. It is also read: (ليُخرِجَ النّاسَ) (li-yukhrija al-nas), with the verb in the third person, meaning that He may bring mankind out. ﴿from the darknesses﴾, that is, so that through it He may bring mankind out of the beliefs of disbelief and misguidance, all of which are pure darknesses and sheer ignorance.

﴿to the light﴾, that is, to the truth which is pure light, but not in just any manner, for you do not guide whomever you love. Rather, it is ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾, that is, by His facilitation and His granting of success. And to indicate that this depends on their turning towards the truth, as is made clear by God Most High's saying: ﴿and guides to Him whoever turns back [in repentance]﴾, the word "permission" (idhn) is used metaphorically for it. "Permission" is an expression for facilitating access to the one who intends to enter. The name "Lord" (rabb) is attributed to their pronoun, which makes clear the nurturing (tarbiyah), which is an expression for bringing a thing to its perfection toward which it is directed. The inclusiveness of permission in this sense for all is clear. On this depends the fact that the sending down was for bringing them all out, and the non-realization of permission in fact for some of them, because its condition, which rests on their bad choice, was not realized, does not harm this. The letter "ya'" (in "bi-idhni") is connected to "tukhrija," or to an implied verb that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its object, that is: "being bound up with the permission of their Lord." Making it a circumstantial clause from its subject is ruled out by the attribution of "Lord" to them and not to Him.

Since the truth, although clear in itself and making things clear to others, leads to God, Mighty and Majestic, the light is used for it metaphorically at one time, and the path at another. So it is said: ﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾, in the manner of substitution (ibdal) by repeating the governing word, as in God Most High's saying: ﴿to those who were deemed weak, to those among them who believed﴾. The omission of the substitute (badal) and the explanation by metaphor (isti'arah) occur in reality, not in figurative usage, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread, [at dawn]﴾. It is also said: it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) founded on a question, as if it were said: "To which light?" So it was said: ﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾. The attribution of "path" to Him, Exalted, is because He is its destination, or because He is the one who makes it clear. Specifying the two attributes by mention is to encourage travel upon it, by explaining what it contains of security and a praiseworthy outcome.

﴿اللَّهِ﴾ in the genitive is an explanatory apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*) to ﴿الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ﴾, because it has come to function like proper names (*aʿlām*), which are dominant through being used exclusively for the God who is worthy of worship in truth, like "the star" used for al-Thurayya (the Pleiades). It was also read in the nominative, as "He is Allah," meaning: the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, the One to whom the path is ascribed. ﴿الَّذِي لَهُ﴾ means in ownership (*mulkan*) and in possession (*milkan*). ﴿مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَمَا فِي الْأَرْضِ﴾ means whatever exists within them, inside them, or outside them, residing in them, as was explained in the verse of the Throne (*Ayat al-Kursi*). On both readings, this explains the great magnitude of the status of the path and shows that following it is binding upon all people without exception. Permitting the nominative as an inceptive subject (*ibtidaʾ*), with the relative clause as its predicate, is based on overlooking this subtle point.

﴿وَوَيْلٌ لِلْكَافِرِينَ﴾ is a threat against those who disbelieve in the Book and do not, through it, bring people out of the darkness into the light. *Wayl* is the opposite of *wal*, which means salvation. Its original form is the accusative, like all verbal nouns (*masadir*), but it was put in the nominative, as with the nominative in its use, to indicate permanence, as in *salamun ʿalayka* (peace be upon you).

﴿مِنْ عَذَابٍ شَدِيدٍ﴾ is connected to *wayl*, in the sense that they wail and cry out because of it, saying, "Alas for us!" This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿دَعَوْا هُنَالِكَ ثُبُورًا﴾ (They will call there for destruction).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 3:

﴿Those who prefer the worldly life﴾ i.e., they give it precedence (yu'thirunaha). It is of the form istif'al from al-mahabba (love), for one who gives preference to one thing over another is as if he seeks of himself that it be more beloved to it (the thing) and more excellent in its sight than other than it.

﴿over the Hereafter﴾ i.e., the eternal Hereafter life.

﴿and who bar⁠﴾ [people] ﴿from the path of God﴾, the path whose matter has been explained. Limiting the reference to the Name of Majesty, which encompasses every beautiful attribute, is for the sake of brevity; the verb is from saddahu, sadd(an). It has been read (yusiddun) from asadda, the transitive form derived from saddа, sudud(an), meaning "to be afflicted" (nakaba); but this is not eloquent, like awqafa. For in its sadd and its waqf there is sufficient alternative to the strain of an unusual derivation.

﴿and who seek it﴾ i.e., they seek for it (yabghuna lahā), so the preposition is elided and the verb is connected directly to the pronoun, i.e., they seek for it ﴿crookedness﴾, i.e., deviation and bending. And it is farthest of all from that. That is, they say to whoever they wish to bar and lead astray: indeed it is a path that is deviating, straying, not upright. The place of the relative clauses of these predicates is in the genitive case, either as an apposition to "the disbelievers" or as an attribute of it. Thus each attribute of theirs is weighed against what corresponds to it of the meanings regarded in the Path: disbelief, which indicates concealment, is set against its being light; preferring the transient worldly life, which discloses the baneful outcome, is set against its conduct being of praiseworthy outcome; and barring from it is set against its being safe. In this there is an indication of their persistence in error that is not hidden. Alternatively, it is in the accusative case by way of dispraise, or in the nominative case as a new subject. The predicate is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those are in far-off error﴾. On the first (reading), it is a resumptive sentence, occurring as a causal explanation for what preceded regarding the befalling of woe upon them, as an emphasis on what the construction of the ruling upon the relative pronoun implies; i.e., those are the ones described with the aforementioned vices: preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter, barring people from the upright path of God, and describing it as crooked. And they are, from that, far removed, in error from the way of truth, far, reaching in that the ultimate extreme of remoteness. Although distance is among the states of the one who is astray, it has been attributed to him figuratively for the sake of emphasis, as in "his fortune has become fortunate" (jadda jadduhu) and "a calamity that is calamitous" (dahiya dahyā'). It is also permissible that the meaning be "in error of one who is distant," or "in it is distance," for the one who is astray may stray from the way at a near place, and may stray far. And in making error encompass them, like the encompassing of a container over what is in it, there is an exaggeration that is not hidden.

(p-32) ﴿And We never sent a messenger﴾, i.e., to the earlier nations before you, as will be mentioned in summary.

﴿except [speaking] in the tongue of his people﴾, i.e., speaking in the language of those to whom he was sent from among the nations that agree on a common language in which he was first raised. It is also read as (bilisn) [with the same meaning], which is a dialect of it, like rish and riyash, and bilusun [with two dammas and a damma with sukun], like 'umud and 'umd.

﴿so that he might make [it] clear to them﴾ what they were commanded, so that they might take it from him with ease and speed, and act upon its requirement without need for translation from one who was not commanded with it. And since this principle could not be observed concerning our master Muhammad ﷺ, and upon all of them, because his mission was general to both jinn and mankind, all of them, despite the differences in their languages, and since the multiplicity of the arrangements of the Book revealed to him, according to the multiplicity of the tongues of the nations, would have been more conducive to dispute, discord of word, and the opening of the hands of distortion, and since the independence of some of that in miraculousness apart from the others would be a cause for detractors to find fault, and the agreement of all upon it is something close to compulsion, and the restriction of clarification to translation and interpretation, wisdom required the unity of the arrangement, which indicates might and the greatness of its status, and which entails rich benefits that are independent of clarification. Moreover, the need for translation multiplies with multiplicity, since each nation must have knowledge that matches the whole and corresponds to it exactly, without any deviation, even in a single unique trait; this is only achieved through one who translates from all of them, singly or in multiplicity, and in this there is such difficulty as nearly amounts to impossibility. Then, since the noblest of peoples, and the most deserving of his call, peace be upon him, was his own people among whom he was sent, and their language is the best of languages, the Mighty Book was revealed in a clear Arabic tongue, and its rulings spread among all nations. It has been said: the pronoun in "his people" refers to Muhammad ﷺ, for God Most High revealed all the books in Arabic, then Jibril, peace be upon him, translated them; or [it refers to] every prophet to whom revelation came, in the language of the people to whom he was sent. This is refuted by His saying, "so that he might make [it] clear to them," for the pronoun refers to the people, and it is evident that not all the books were revealed to clarify for the Arabs; and in returning it to the people of each prophet, it is as if it were said: "And We did not send any messenger except in the tongue of the people of Muhammad ﷺ so that the messenger might make clear to his people to whom he was sent," which involves an obvious strain.

﴿So God leads astray whom He wills﴾, i.e., leaving him to go astray: He creates misguidance in him by his engaging in its causes that lead to it, or He forsakes him and does not show him kindness, because He knows that kindness will not benefit him.

﴿and guides whom He wills﴾ with success and bestowing of kindnesses, guidance for him because of his turning in repentance and his turning toward the truth. The shift to attributing the two verbs to the glorious Name that encompasses the attributes is to magnify their matter and to highlight the basis of each of them. The fa' is an eloquent conjunction, like it in His saying, "Then We said: Strike the sea with your staff, and it split" (Q 26:63). It is as if it were said: "So they made it clear to them, and God led astray from among them whom He willed to lead astray, by what befits none but Him, and guided whom He willed to guide, because of his deserving it." The omission is to indicate that the eagerness of each messenger to do what he was commanded, and the course of each of those who are forsaken and those who are guided according to His way, is a certain matter, independent of mention and explanation. The shift to the present form is to bring the scene to mind, or to indicate renewal and continuity, in accordance with the renewal of clarification by the successive messengers, peace be upon them. The mention of misguidance before guidance is either because it is the continuation of what was as it was, while guidance is the creation of what was not, or to stress the point that clarification and reminder by the messengers have no effect, and that the matter depends entirely on His will, Most High, by suggesting that the consequence of misguidance upon that is swifter than the consequence of being guided. This confirms what preceded concerning the restriction of bringing out from darknesses into light to the permission of God Most High.

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, so none can overpower Him in His will, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does not do anything of misguidance or guidance except for a far-reaching wisdom. In this is the indication that what was entrusted to the messengers is only the conveying of the message and the clarification of the path of truth, while guidance and directing to it are in the hand of God, glorified is He, who does what He wills and decrees what He desires.

**﴿And We certainly sent Moses﴾**: This begins the detailed explanation of what was stated in summary in His words, Exalted and Majestic be He: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except with the language of his people, so that he might make [it] clear to them﴾, and so on.

**﴿with Our signs﴾**: That is, accompanied by them. These are his miracles, which He manifested to the Children of Israel.

**﴿that bring out your people﴾**: Here *an* is interpreted as *ay* (an explanatory particle, "that" or "namely"), because sending (*irsal*) contains the sense of saying. Alternatively, it is the *an* of the verbal-noun sense (*an* with a verb in the subjunctive, meaning "to"), as in His words, Exalted be He: ﴿And that you set your face﴾. The forms of verbs are equivalent in indicating the verbal noun, and this is the basis for the correctness of the connection (*al-wasl*, the grammatical linking of the clause). What is meant is the bringing out of the Children of Israel after the destruction of Pharaoh, ﴿from the darknesses﴾, that is, from disbelief and the ignorance that led them to say: "O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods."

**﴿into the light﴾**: That is, into faith in God, His unity, and all the other things they were commanded to do.

**﴿And remind them of the Days of God﴾**: That is, of His blessings and His trials, as His words indicate: "﴿Remember the blessing of God upon you﴾." However, this is not limited to what befell them alone, but includes them and the nations before them in the bygone days, as His words, Exalted be He, indicate: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you?﴾ and the verses that follow. Or it means His days that contain these things, as His words indicate: ﴿when He saved you﴾. The shift from the first person (speaking) to the third person (absent) by attributing the days to the Divine Name (*al-ism al-jalil*, the Name of Majesty, Allah), is to indicate the grandeur of their station and to signal that the dealings contained in them are not specific to the addressee and his people, as the attribution to the pronoun of the speaker might suggest. That is: admonish them with encouragement, warning, promise, and threat. It has also been said: "The Days of God" are His events that befell the nations before them, and "the Days of the Arabs" are their battles, wars, and great conflicts. That is: warn them of His events that overtook the nations that had gone before. This is refuted by what he, ﷺ, undertook in readiness to comply, namely reminding them of both ease and hardship, of what befell them and others, as is recited to you.

**﴿Surely in that﴾**: That is, in the reminding of them, or in the totality of those blessings and trials, or in their days.

**﴿are signs﴾**: great, or numerous, indicating the oneness of God, His power, His knowledge, and His wisdom. According to the first interpretation, the signs are the days themselves, whether what is meant is the days in themselves or what is in them of blessings and trials. The meaning of the reminding being "in" them (the days) is that it is the occasion for their becoming manifest. According to the third interpretation, the signs are those blessings and trials, and the meaning of "in" is clear. As for the second interpretation, that the demonstrative refers to the totality of the blessings, then "in" means "from" regarding each one of those blessings and trials; the referent is the totality, which includes them insofar as it is a totality. Or the word *fi* ("in") is *tajridiyya* (of abstraction, used to introduce the sense of a specific thing from which the object is abstracted), similar to its use in His words, Exalted be He: ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity﴾.

**﴿for every steadfast one﴾** in His trials, **﴿grateful﴾** for His blessings. It has also been said: "for every believer." The expression of them by this is to signal that patience and gratitude are the hallmark of the believer; that is, for everyone who is worthy of the perfection of patience and gratitude, or faith, and whose affair comes to them, not merely for one who has actually attained these qualities. This is because it is a justification for the preceding command to remind, leading to that rank, since whoever remembers what has overflowed upon him, or descended upon him, or upon those before him, of blessings and trials, and becomes alert to the outcome of gratitude and patience, or faith, will scarcely be parted from them. The restriction of the signs to them is because they are the ones who benefit from them, not because they are hidden from others, since the clarification is achieved in relation to all. The placement of "steadfast" before "grateful" is due to the precedence of the object of patience, namely trials, over the object of gratitude, namely blessings, and because gratitude is the outcome of patience.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 6:

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾ This begins an account of how he (peace be upon him) took up the task he was commanded to carry out, namely reminding them of the aforementioned deliverance. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object, governed by a hidden verb addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ). The attachment of the reminder to a time, even though the real aim is to remind them of the events that took place in that time, has had its wisdom explained more than once. The meaning is: remind them of the time when he (peace be upon him) said to his people: ﴿Remember the blessing of God upon you﴾. He (peace be upon him) began with encouragement, because it is more readily received by the soul, and the soul inclines towards it. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected either to the blessing itself, if "ni'ma" is taken as a verbal noun (masdar), or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, if "ni'ma" is taken as a noun. In that case the meaning is: remember His favour upon you, or remember the blessing as it was bestowed upon you. Likewise the word "idh" in the words of the Exalted: ﴿when He delivered you from the people of Fir'awn (Pharaoh)﴾, meaning: remember His favour upon you at the time when He delivered you from the people of Fir'awn; or remember the blessing of God as established upon you at the time when He delivered you from them. Or it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion, a apposition where the second term is included within the first) of "the blessing of God", where "blessing" means favour or gift.

﴿They inflict upon you﴾: "yasumunakum" means they seek to impose upon you, from "sama-hu khasfan", when one inflicts injustice upon him. The root sense of "sawm" is going forth in pursuit of something.

﴿evil torment﴾: "su'" is the verbal noun of "sa'a yasu'u" (to be evil/to harm). It means either the kind of torment that is evil in itself, or their abasement of you, their employing you in arduous labour, their humiliation of you, and other things that cannot be enumerated. It is in the accusative because it is the object of "yasumunakum".

﴿and slaughter your sons﴾: meaning the male infants who were born. He joined this to "they inflict upon you" in order to remove it from the category of ordinary torment. They did this because Fir'awn either saw in a dream, or was told by the soothsayers, that a male child would be born among them who would bring about the end of his kingdom. So they exerted themselves in this, but it did not avail them anything against the decree of God.

﴿and spare your women﴾: meaning they keep them alive in life, but in humiliation and degradation. For this reason it is counted among the afflictions. The clauses are circumstantial qualifiers (ahwal) either of "the people of Fir'awn", or of the pronoun of the addressees, or of both together, because each of them is contained in them as a pronoun.

﴿And in that﴾: meaning in what was mentioned of their monstrous deeds ﴿there was a trial from your Lord﴾: meaning a testing from Him, not that the trial is identical with those deeds. The exception is that you may take "fi" as tajrida (abstraction, a figurative sense in which the preposition expresses that the thing is stripped of its own essence), and then its attribution to God the Exalted is either in respect of creation, or of empowering and enabling.

﴿great﴾: that cannot be borne. It is also permissible that what is referred to is the deliverance from that, and the trial is the testing by means of blessing. This second reading is the more fitting, as the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) hints at it. On the first reading, that is considered in terms of its outcome, which is deliverance, or in terms of the fact that the trial of a believer is a form of upbringing (tarbiya) for him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 7:

﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is part of what Musa (peace be upon him) said to his people. It is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "the favour of Allah," meaning: remember the favour of Allah upon you, and remember when your Lord proclaimed (ta'adhdhana), that is, He proclaimed with an emphatic proclamation (idhanan baligan), leaving no trace of doubt with it, because of what the form tafa''ala (taf'ul) carries of the meaning of exertion (takalluf), which, when attributed to Him, glorified is He, is taken to its ultimate end, which is perfection. It was also said: it is coordinated with His statement, exalted is He, "when He delivered you" (idh anjakum), meaning: remember His favour, exalted is He, in these two times, for this proclamation too is a favour from Allah, exalted is He, upon them, by which they attain the good of this world and the Hereafter. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "And when your Lord said." Musa (peace be upon him) first reminded them explicitly of Allah's blessings upon them (p-35), and included in this a reminder of the afflictions that had befallen them before that. Then he commanded them, a second time, to remember what Allah, glorified is He, had decreed of the promise of increase upon gratitude and the threat of punishment upon disbelief. By "reminding of the times" is meant reminding of the events that occurred in them in detail, since those times encompass them; when they are mentioned, what is in them is mentioned as though it were witnessed and observed.

﴿If you are grateful﴾, O Children of Israel, for what I have bestowed upon you of the favour of deliverance, the destruction of the enemy, and other blessings and graces that are beyond enumeration, and you respond to it with faith and obedience.

﴿I will surely increase you﴾ in favour upon favour. ﴿But if you are ungrateful﴾ for that, and disdain it, ﴿indeed My punishment is severe﴾; so perhaps there will befall you from it what will befall you. It is a custom of the noble to state promise explicitly and to allude to threat. So what is your thought of the Most Noble of the noble? It is also permissible that what is mentioned be an explanation of the omitted answer, meaning: "I will surely punish you." The lam in both places is a preparatory lam for an oath, and each of the two answers stands in place of the answers of both the condition and the oath. The clause is either an object of ta'adhdhana, since it is a kind of speech, or of a speech implied after it, as if it were said: "And when your Lord proclaimed," so He said: ... etc.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 8:

﴿And Moses said: If you disbelieve﴾, [i.e., disbelieve] in His blessings, exalted is He, and do not give thanks for them, ﴿you and whoever is on the earth, all of them﴾ [of the creatures], ﴿then indeed Allah is Free of need﴾ [i.e., independent] of your thanks and the thanks of others, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, deserving of praise in His essence, because of the abundance of the favours that necessitate it from Him, even if no one praises Him; or He is the Praised One, whom the angels praise. Rather, every atom of the world speaks of His praise. Praise, wherever it occurs in return for a blessing or other virtues, is more indicative of His perfection, glory be to Him. This is an explanation of what has been omitted from the answer to "if" (in). That is: if you disbelieve, its consequence returns only to you, for indeed Allah, exalted is He, is Free of need of the thanks of those who give thanks. Perhaps he, peace be upon him, said this when he observed from them signs of obstinacy and indications of persistence in disbelief and corruption, and he became certain that encouragement would not benefit them, nor would an allusion to intimidation. Or he said it after reminding them of the words of Allah, mighty is His authority, and to affirm its content and warn them against ingratitude; then he began to intimidate them by reminding them of what befell the earlier nations, and said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 9:

﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you﴾ so that they may reflect upon what befell each of the two parties, the believers and the disbelievers, and then desist from the evil they are engaged in and turn in repentance to Allah, Exalted is He. It has also been said: this is the beginning of a speech from Allah, Exalted is He, addressed to the disbelievers in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. In that case, the reminder of Musa, peace be upon him, concerns what was specific to the Children of Israel of adversity and ease, and the days are the days that passed over them alone. But there is in this what is not hidden of remoteness. Moreover, in that case it does not become clear why the disbelievers of the time of the Prophet ﷺ are singled out for reminder with what befell those enumerated, although others are an example for them in having passed away before them. ﴿The people of Nuh﴾ is a substitute for the relative pronoun, or an explanatory apposition. ﴿And ʿAd﴾ is coordinated with the people of Nuh. ﴿And Thamud, and those after them﴾, that is, of those mentioned, is a general coordination with the people of Nuh and what is coordinated with it. His, Exalted is He, saying ﴿None knows them but Allah﴾ is a parenthetical clause, or the relative pronoun is the subject, and "none knows them" through to its end is its predicate, and the sentence is a parenthetical clause. The meaning is that they are so numerous that none knows their number except Allah, glorified is He. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that between ʿAdnan and Isma'il there are thirty fathers who are not known. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say when he recited this verse: "The genealogists have lied," meaning that they claim knowledge of lineages, while Allah, Exalted is He, has negated their knowledge from the servants.

﴿Their messengers came to them﴾ is a resumptive statement explaining their news ﴿with clear proofs﴾, with manifest miracles and dazzling signs. Each messenger made clear to his community the way of truth and guided them to it, so as to bring them out of darkness into light.

﴿So they put their hands to their mouths﴾, gesturing thereby toward their tongues and what issues from them of speech, out of concern on their part for its matter and as an admonition to the messengers to receive it and guard it, and to despair them of belief and assent, by informing them that there is no answer for them other than this.

﴿And they said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, that is, according to your claim, and it refers to the clear proofs which they presented as evidence for the validity of their missions. Like His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿And We indeed sent Musa with Our signs﴾. Their intended meaning by "disbelieving in it" is disbelief in its indication of the validity of their missions. Or they bit their hands out of rage and vexation at what the messengers brought, like His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾. Or they placed them upon their mouths out of wonder at it and in mockery of it, like one overcome by laughter. Or to silence the prophets, peace be upon them, and to command them to close their mouths. Or they put them into the mouths of the prophets, peace be upon them, preventing them from speaking, either in reality or figuratively. Or they made the hands of the prophets go into their mouths out of wonder at their obstinacy and stubbornness, as their saying indicates: ﴿Is there doubt about Allah...﴾ etc. It has also been said: "al-aydi" here means "al-ayadi" (blessings), and it is expressed by it for their admonitions, their advice, and their laws, on which the religious and worldly blessings depend, because when they denied them and did not accept them, it was as if they returned them to the place from which they had come.

﴿And indeed we are in grave doubt﴾

﴿concerning that to which you invite us﴾ of belief in Allah and monotheism. Thus their doubt regarding that does not contradict their definitive disbelief in what the messengers were sent with of clear proofs, for they disbelieved in them definitively, in that they did not regard them as significant and did not count them among the kind of miracles; and for this reason they said: ﴿So bring us a manifest authority﴾. It is also read "tadda'una" with assimilation. ﴿Disquieting﴾, causing unease, from "arabahu" (he made him doubtful), or possessing doubt, from "araba al-rajulu," and it is the restlessness of the soul and its non-tranquility regarding a thing.

﴿Their messengers said﴾ is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as if it were said: "What did their messengers say to them?" The answer is that they said this, denouncing them and marvelling at their foolish statement.

﴿Is there doubt about God?﴾ The interrogative particle *hamza* is placed before the adverbial phrase to indicate that the object of the denial is not doubt itself, but its occurrence regarding a matter where doubt is hardly conceivable at all. This follows the response's conformity to the wording of the disbelievers, who would say, "Are you in dubious doubt about God, may He be exalted?" The messengers responded in this way to emphasise the exalted majesty of the Glorified One as free from any trace of doubt, and to record against them the feebleness of their minds. That is: is there any doubt concerning His affair, whether His existence, His oneness, or the obligation to believe in Him alone? It is the most manifest of all manifest things and the clearest of all clear things, so that you would be in dubious doubt from His side. Since their ultimate aim was the call to faith and monotheism, and the manifestation of the clear proofs was a means to this, they did not address the disbelievers' statement, "We have disbelieved in what you were sent with," but confined themselves to explaining what is the supreme goal. Then they followed this denial with what necessitates it of the evidences indicating the non-existence of what is denied.

So they said: ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the one who brought them into being, and what is in them of created things arranged in exquisite order, which bears witness to the reality of that about which you are in doubt. This phrase is an adjective (*ṣifah*) of the majestic Name, or an apposition (*badal*) to it. The word "doubt" is raised by the adverbial phrase because it depends on the interrogation. Making it the subject, with the adverb as its predicate, would lead to separating the described and its description by a foreign element, namely the subject, whereas the agent is not foreign to its governing word; and this has also been permitted.

﴿He calls you﴾ to belief through His sending us, not as though we call you to it of our own accord, as your saying "that which you call us to" might suggest. ﴿That He may forgive you﴾ some of your sins by means of it, or He calls you for the sake of forgiveness, as in your saying: "I invited him so that he might eat with me."

﴿Some of your sins﴾, that is, some of them: namely, all except the wrongs between you and other people, for Islam wipes out what came before it. It has been said that this is how it occurs throughout the Qur'an in the promise made to the disbelievers, not the promise made to the believers, to distinguish between the two promises. Perhaps this is because forgiveness, wherever it comes in address to the disbelievers, is linked to pure faith, whereas regarding the believers it is accompanied by obedience, avoidance of sins, and the like, so that it encompasses the removal of wrongs. It has also been said that the meaning is: that He may forgive you instead of your sins.

﴿And defer you until a named term﴾, until a time which God, exalted is He, has named and made the end of your lifespans, on the condition of faith.

﴿They said﴾ is a resumptive clause as previously mentioned.

﴿You are only﴾, that is, you are not anything except ﴿mortals like us﴾, without any superiority that qualifies you for what you claim of prophethood, ﴿you want﴾. This is a second adjective of "mortals," construed according to meaning, as in God's words, ﴿Shall mere mortals guide us?﴾ Alternatively it is a new independent clause, meaning: you intend by what you undertake of the call and guidance,

﴿to turn us away﴾ by singling out worship for God, glorified is He, ﴿from what our fathers used to worship﴾, that is, from worshipping what our fathers continued to worship without any reason requiring it. ﴿Otherwise, bring us﴾, that is, if the matter is not as we say, but you are indeed messengers from God, exalted is He, as you claim, then bring us ﴿a manifest authority﴾ that demonstrates your superiority and your worthiness of that rank, or demonstrates the soundness of what you claim of prophethood, so that we may abandon what we have not ceased to worship, generation after generation. Indeed, they had been brought clear signs and dazzling proofs, such that the deaf mountains would crumble before them; but they only say what they say of enormities out of stubbornness, obstinacy, and a show for those behind them, that this is not of the kind to which the title "manifest authority" applies.

﴿Their messengers said to them﴾, responding in kind to the opening of their statement. The address was specifically to them, because the speech was directed at them with the aim of holding them to account. This differs from what preceded it, the denial that there is any doubt about God, glorified be He, since that is a general matter, even though what follows it is specific to them.

﴿It is not that we are anything but humans like you﴾, as you say, ﴿but God bestows favour﴾ of prophethood ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾. They mean that this is a gift from God, Exalted is He, given to whomever He wills of His servants purely by grace and bounty, without any cause that would make it obligatory. They said this out of humility and self-abasement. Or it means: we are not angels, but we are humans like you in form, or in belonging to the same species. ﴿But God bestows﴾ virtues, perfections and capacities, ﴿upon whomever He wills to bestow favour upon﴾. He wills this only because He knows that the person deserves them. These virtues, perfections and capacities are what the sphere of selection for prophethood revolves around.

﴿And it was not for us﴾, that is, it was not right or proper for us, ﴿to bring you any authority﴾, that is, any proof of the proofs, let alone a clear authority regarding any matter or by any means.

﴿Except by the permission of God﴾, for this is a matter dependent on His will, Exalted is He. If He wills it, it occurs; otherwise it does not. ﴿And upon God﴾ alone, to the exclusion of anything else absolutely, ﴿let the believers rely﴾. This is a command from them to the believers to rely upon God, and their intention is to direct their own souls towards this, which is the most effective means of doing so. Do you not see the words of Him, Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 12:

﴿And what [excuse] do we have﴾ i.e., what excuse do we have ﴿that we should not put our trust in Allah﴾ i.e., regarding [the matter of] not putting our trust in Him. The [explicit mention of the Name] "Allah" is for the purpose of displaying eagerness to trust in Him, of delighting in mentioning His name, and of giving the reason for trusting [in Him].

﴿And He has indeed guided us﴾ i.e., and the situation is that He has indeed done to us what necessitates and calls for [trust], in that He has guided us

﴿to our paths﴾ i.e., He has guided each of us to his own way and his own method, which was prescribed for him, and made it obligatory upon him to follow it in religion. Since the harm inflicted by the disbelievers is something that causes anxiety and agitation, which undermine trust, they said, by way of emphatic oath, displaying complete resolve: ﴿And we will surely endure patiently whatever harm you inflict upon us﴾ through obstinacy, through demanding signs, and other things in which there is no good.

﴿And upon Allah alone﴾ ﴿let those who [truly] put their trust rely﴾ i.e., let the trusting ones remain steadfast in the trust they have established. The intended meaning is the same as what preceded: the obligation of trusting in Allah on their own part. By "those who put their trust" is meant the believers, and the expression of them by this description is because their being characterized by it was mentioned earlier. It is also permissible that the intended meaning be: and upon Him let whoever trusts rely, to the exclusion of anyone else.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 13:

﴿And those who disbelieved said⁠ ﴾ — perhaps these speakers are some of the rebellious, obstinate ones who were extreme in disbelief among those disbelieving nations whose shameful sayings were transmitted, rather than all of them, such as the people of Shu'ayb and their likes. For this reason it does not say: ﴿and they said⁠ ﴾ — "to their messengers: ﴿We will surely expel you from our land, or you will return to our religion (millah)⁠ ﴾." They were not content with their disobedience to the messengers and their obstinate opposition to the truth after they had seen the clear signs, which are too evident to be limited, until they dared to [say] such a monstrous thing as cannot be encompassed by the realm of possibility. So they swore that one of the two alternatives would happen. The "return" (al-'awd) is either in the general sense of becoming (mutlaq al-sayrurah), or in terms of the believers' dominance over the messengers, as has been discussed in al-A'raf, and will come in al-Kahf. ﴿Then their Lord revealed to them⁠ ﴾ — that is, to the messengers, ﴿their Lord⁠ ﴾, the Master of their affair, when the disbelief of the disbelievers reached its limit and they attained such defiance that there is no hope for their faith thereafter — ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers⁠ ﴾. This is either by implying a verb of speech, or by treating the revelation as if it were a kind of speech (since it is a form of it).

And We will surely settle you in the land after them. That is, their land and their dwellings, as a punishment for them for their saying, "We will surely expel you from our land." It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ [al-A'raf 7:137]. ﴿After them﴾ means: after their destruction. It is also recited as (la-yuhlikanna) and (la-yuskinannakum) with the ya' (third person), taking into account "awha" (He revealed). It is like the saying: Zayd swore that he would surely go out tomorrow. ﴿That﴾ refers to what was revealed, namely the destruction of the wrongdoers and the settling of the believers in their dwellings. That is: this matter is certain and established.

﴿For him who fears My standing﴾ (p-39) — My station. It is the station in which the servants stand on the day when people stand before the Lord of the worlds; or it means My standing over him and My guarding of his deeds. It has been said that the word "maqam" here is superfluous (muqhamun). ﴿And fears My threat﴾ — My threat of punishment, or My promised punishment for the disbelievers. The meaning is: that this is a truth for the God-fearing, like His saying: "And the good end is for the God-fearing."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 15:**

﴿And they sought victory﴾, that is, they sought God's help against their enemies, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you seek a victory, then the victory has certainly come to you﴾. Or [it means] they sought a ruling (istahkamu), and asked Him for judgment between them, from al-fataha (judgment), which is ḥukūma (arbitration, judgment). Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with the truth﴾. The pronoun [in "they sought"] refers to the Messengers, and it is said: to the disbelievers. And it is said: to both parties. For they asked that the one who is right be helped and the one who is false be destroyed. It is coordinated with "He revealed to them" (awḥā ilayhim), and it has been recited in the imperative form, coordinated with "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers". That is: their Lord revealed to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers," and said to them, "Seek victory." ﴿And every obstinate tyrant failed﴾, that is, lost and perished, ﴿every obstinate tyrant﴾, characterized by the opposite of what the God-fearing are characterized by. That is: they were helped when they sought victory, attained what they asked for and prospered, and every obstinate tyrant failed, and they are their own people who were stubbornly opposed. So "failure" here means general deprivation, not merely deprivation of the sought object. Or that is in consideration of the fact that they used to claim that they were upon the truth. Or the disbelievers sought victory against the Messengers and failed, and did not prosper. It was only said, "And every obstinate tyrant failed," as a censure of them and a recording against them of tyranny and obstinacy, and not that some of them were not like that, nor that failure did not befall them. Or they all sought victory, so the Messengers were helped and their promise was fulfilled, and every transgressor, rebellious one failed. So "failure" means deprivation after seeking. And in attributing failure to each of them there is an exaggeration that is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 16:

﴿Before him is Hell﴾. That is: in front of him. For he is kept under watch for it, standing on its brink in the world, and sent forth to it in the Hereafter. It has also been said: "from behind his life"; and its reality is what is hidden from you.

﴿And he will be made to drink﴾ is conjoined to an implied clause, serving as an answer to the question of a questioner, as if it were said: "What will happen then?" So it is said: he will be cast into it, and he will be made to drink ﴿from water﴾ of a particular kind, unlike the waters that are familiar.

﴿Pus (sadid)﴾, which is matter (qayh), or blood mixed with pus (midda) flowing from a wound. Mujahid and others said: it is what flows from the bodies of the people of the Fire. It is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to what was left vague at first, then clarified by "pus" to magnify its gravity. Singling it out for mention from among its punishments indicates that it is among the most severe of its kinds.

﴿He will gulp it down﴾. It was said: this is a description of water, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to it. The more apparent view is that it is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) answering an implied question, as if it were said: "What is done with it?" and the answer was: "He will gulp it down," meaning that he will force himself to swallow it again and again, because of the overpowering thirst and the heat that has taken hold of him.

﴿And he will hardly be able to swallow it﴾: that is, he will not come close to swallowing it, let alone swallow it easily. Rather, he will choke on it, and so he will drink it, after much struggle, one sip after another, so his punishment is prolonged at one time by the heat and thirst, and at another time by drinking it in that state. Swallowing (*siwāgh*) is the smooth passage of a drink down the throat, with ease and the soul's acceptance. Its negation does not necessarily negate everything mentioned together. It was also said: he will hardly be able to bring it into his stomach, and it was expressed as "swallowing" because that is what is customary with drinks. This clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "he will gulp it down," or to its object, or to both together.

﴿And death will come to him﴾: that is, its causes from hardships, ﴿from every place﴾, and it will surround him from all directions, or from every place in his body, even from the roots of his hair and the tip of his big toe.

﴿Yet he will not be dead﴾: that is, while the actual state is that he is not truly dead, as the apparent meaning from the coming of its causes would suggest, especially from all directions, so that he does not feel pain from the kinds of destructive things that overwhelm him.

﴿And behind him﴾: that is, before him, ﴿there is a severe punishment﴾, which receives at every moment a punishment harsher and more difficult than what came before it. In this there is a rebuttal of the notion that he might become accustomed to it and feel it less, as with the punishments of this world. It was also said that it is eternal abiding in the Fire. It was also said that it is the holding of breath. It was also said that what is meant by "seeking victory" and "failure" is the rain-seeking of the people of Makkah in their years of drought which Allah sent upon them, in answer to the prayer of the Messenger (ﷺ) against them, and their failure in that; and He promised them, instead of that, the pus of the people of the Fire.

The likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord (﴿مَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾): that is, their description and their strange condition, which is itself like a likeness in its wondrousness. It is a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence), whose predicate (khabar) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿أعْمالُهم كَرَمادٍ﴾ ("their deeds are like ashes"), as in your saying: "the description of Zayd is that his honour is violated and his wealth is plundered." This is an isti'naf (resumptive new sentence) answering the question of one who asks: "What is the matter with their deeds, which they performed in the ways of righteousness, such as maintaining the ties of kinship, freeing slaves, ransoming captives, relieving the distressed, hospitality to guests, and other things of the category of noble conduct, that their affair has come to this end?" So it is answered: "Those deeds are like ashes, ﴿اشْتَدَّتْ بِهِ الرِّيحُ﴾ ("the wind blew violently upon it"), carrying it away and hastening its departure, ﴿فِي يَوْمٍ عاصِفٍ﴾ ("on a stormy day"). Al-'asf (the 'asf) is the intensification of the wind, and it is attributed to its time as an intensification, as in your saying: "a night of drunkenness" (laylatun sakirah), whereas the intoxication actually belongs to its wind. Their deeds, which were counted, since they were built on no foundation of knowledge of God, Exalted is He, of faith in Him, and of directing them towards Him, are likened to ashes which the violent wind has scattered.

Alternatively, it is a resumptive sentence presented to explain their deeds for the idols; or it is a mubtada' whose khabar is omitted, as is the view of Sibawayh, meaning: "in what is recited to you is their likeness." His saying "a'maluhum" (their deeds) is a resumptive sentence built on the question of one who asks: "How is their likeness?" It is answered: "Their deeds are such and such," whether by "their deeds" is meant their handiwork or their deeds done for their idols. It has also been said that "a'maluhum" is a badal (substitute) for "mathalu alladhina" (the likeness of those who). His saying "ka-ramad" (like ashes) is the khabar.

﴿لا يَقْدِرُونَ﴾ ("they will have no power"), that is, on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿مِمّا كَسَبُوا﴾ ("over what they earned") from those deeds, ﴿عَلى شَيْءٍ﴾ ("anything"), that is, they will not see any trace of reward or lightening of punishment from them, in the manner of the mentioned ashes. This is the summation (fadhlakah) of the likeness. And restricting the statement to the non-seeing of any effect of their deeds for the idols, although the idols have dreadful punishments, is to make explicit the invalidity of their belief and their claim that the idols are intercessors for them with God, Exalted is He. There is also in it a mockery of them.

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ ("That"), that is, what the likeness indicates clearly of their misguidance, together with their assumption that they are upon something, ﴿هُوَ الضَّلالُ البَعِيدُ﴾ ("is the far-reaching error"), far from the path of rightness, or far from attaining reward.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 19:

﴿Have you not seen?﴾ This is an address to the Messenger (peace be upon him), but what is meant is his community (ummah). It has also been said: it is addressed to every disbeliever, due to His saying, exalted is He: "He would take you away" (yudhhibkum), and the seeing here is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that Allah created the heavens and the earth﴾ is a clause standing in place of its two objects (sadd masadd maf'ulayha), that is: Do you not know that He, exalted is He, created them ﴿with truth﴾, combined with wisdom and with the correct manner in which they ought to be created. It has also been read: (Creator of the heavens and the earth). ﴿If He wills, He will take you away﴾, that is, He will annihilate you entirely, ﴿and bring a new creation﴾, that is: He will create in your place a fresh creation with no connection between you and them. He linked His power to that (act) with His power to create the heavens and the earth in this wondrous pattern, as a guide to the method of inference. For whoever is able to create such great bodies is even more able to replace you with another creation. Therefore He said:

**"And that is not difficult for Allah"** — that is, your removal and the bringing of a new creation in your place.

**"is not hard (ʿazīz) for Allah"** — not unattainable or difficult. For He is Able in His essence over all possible things; there is no specificity to Him regarding one object of power over another. One whose condition is this is worthy of being believed in, of having His reward hoped for, and of having His punishment feared.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 21:

﴿And they will come forth before Allah all together﴾ That is: they will come forth on the Day of Resurrection. The use of the past tense form (al-madi) serves to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾. Or it is because, with respect to Him, glorified is He, there is neither past nor future. The meaning is: their emergence from their graves by the command of Allah, the Exalted, and their being called to account; or [it means] "before Allah" according to their own assumption, for when they were committing abominations in secret they used to think that these would remain hidden from Allah, glorified is He. So when the Day of Resurrection comes, they will be exposed before Allah in their own estimation. ﴿Then the weak will say﴾ the followers, the plural of "da'if" (weak), and what is meant is weakness of opinion. It was written with a waw, and in the manner of those who pronounce the alif before the hamza with emphasis (tafkhim). ﴿To those who were arrogant﴾ to their leaders who had made them follow and had misled them, ﴿Indeed, we were﴾ in the world ﴿for you followers﴾ in denying the messengers, peace be upon them, and turning away from their advice. It is a plural of the form "tabi'" (follower), like "ghayb" (unseen) in the plural "ghaib" (unseen things), or a verbal noun described by it for emphasis, or by an elision, meaning: possessors of following.

﴿So will you avail us﴾ be a means of warding off ﴿against us﴾. The fa' (so) indicates that following is the cause of the seeking of relief, and the purpose is rebuke, reproach, censure, and reprimand.

﴿any portion of the punishment of Allah﴾. The first "min" (of) is explanatory (lil-bayan), occurring in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The second "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), occurring in the position of the object, meaning: some part of the thing which is the punishment of Allah, the Exalted. It is permissible for both to be partitive, meaning: some part of a thing which is some part of the punishment of Allah. The i'rab is as previously mentioned. It is also permissible for the first to be the object and the second to be a verbal noun, meaning: will you avail us some part of the punishment with some part of availing? The first interpretation is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So will you avail us a share of the Fire?﴾

﴿They will say﴾ that is, the arrogant, answering the reproach of the followers and offering an excuse for what they had done to them: ﴿Had Allah guided us﴾ that is, to faith and granted us success in it, ﴿we would have guided you﴾. But we went astray, so we led you astray. That is: we chose for you what we chose for ourselves. Or: had Allah guided us to the path of salvation from the punishment, we would have guided you and would have availed you, as we had hoped, but the path of escape was closed to us, and there was no longer any escape (wa-la-ta hina manas). ﴿It is the same for us whether we are distressed﴾ at what we have encountered ﴿or we are patient﴾ regarding it. That is: distress and patience are equal for us in failing to deliver us. The hamza and "am" are for emphasizing the equality, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. They attributed the two to themselves and ascribed their equality to the first-person pronoun which includes the addressees as well, for emphasis in forbidding reproach, by informing them that they are partners with them in what they have been afflicted with, and as consolation for them. It is also permissible that His saying, "It is the same for us..." etc., is from the speech of both groups, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is so that he may know that I did not betray him﴾. This is supported by what is reported: that they will say, "Come, let us be distressed," and they will be distressed for five hundred years, and it will not benefit them. Then they will say, "Come, let us be patient," and they will be patient likewise, and it will not benefit them. At that point they say this. And since the reproach of the followers was of the nature of distress, they appended their answer with a statement that there is no benefit in that. So they said: ﴿For us there is no escape﴾ from a refuge, or a place of flight from the punishment, from "hasa al-himar" when the donkey swerved in fleeing. It is either a noun of place, like "al-mabit" (place of spending the night) and "al-masif" (place of summering), or a verbal noun like "al-maghib" (setting) and "al-mashib" (greying). This is an explanatory clause, elaborating what is implied in the equality. Therefore it has no place in i'rab, or it is a emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal), or a substitute (badal) for it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 14, Verse 22**

﴿And Satan will say﴾, he who misled both groups, and drew them along with him when they reproached him, by what the followers had said to the arrogant, ﴿when the matter has been decided﴾, meaning: it has been firmly settled and concluded, which is the Reckoning, and the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire. He delivers this address (khutbah) in the assembly of the wretched among the two sacred species (humans and jinn).

﴿Indeed, Allah promised you a promise of truth﴾, meaning: a promise whose truth requires that it be fulfilled, so He fulfilled it. Or, a promise that He fulfilled, which is the promise of Resurrection and recompense.

﴿And I promised you﴾, meaning: the promise of falsehood, which is that there is no Resurrection and no recompense. And if there were, then the idols would be your intercessors. He did not explicitly declare its falsehood, because of what his words indicate: ﴿but I broke it to you﴾, meaning: I broke my promise, with the second object omitted, i.e., I annulled it. He made his promise like a breaking of it, as though he had been able to fulfil it, and how could he have been able to do so? ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾, meaning: no power of domination, nor any proof that would indicate the truth of my claim. ﴿Except that I called you﴾, except my calling you to it and my enticement. Although this is not of the category of authority, he presented it in its manifest form, in the manner of [their greeting among them is a painful striking] (a line of poetry), as an exaggeration in negating authority from himself, as though he said: authority over you would belong to me only if mere calling were of its kind. It is also permissible for the exception to be disjunctive (istithna' munqati', an exception not of the same category as what precedes it).

﴿So you responded to me﴾, meaning: you quickly answered me. ﴿So do not blame me﴾ for my promise to you, since it was not in the manner of restriction (qasr, limiting something to a specific condition) or compulsion (ilja', forcing someone), as the fa' (so) indicates. It was recited with the ya' (﴿فَلا تَلُومُونِي﴾ read as ﴿فَلا يَلُومُونِي﴾ ...), in the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until, when you are in the ship and they sail with them﴾. ﴿And blame yourselves﴾, since you responded to me by your own choice when I called you, without any proof or evidence, merely by adornment and enticement. You did not respond to your Lord when He called you with the call of truth, accompanied by clear signs and proofs. His purpose is not to disclaim entirely the blame directed at him, but to show that they are more deserving of it than he is. There is no indication in this for the independence of the servant in his actions, as the Mu'tazila claimed. Rather, it suffices for this that the servant has an acquiring power (qudrah kasibah, the acquisition by which the servant is held responsible) through which the sphere of obligation revolves, and that it has a role in it. For He, glory be to Him, creates His acts according to what He chooses, and upon this happiness and wretchedness are based. As for what has been said: that it would require saying, "so do not blame me, nor yourselves, since Allah decreed disbelief upon you and compelled you to it," this is based on failing to distinguish between the doctrine of the People of Truth and the path of the Jabriyya (determinists who deny human agency).

﴿I cannot help you﴾, meaning: I cannot rescue you from the punishment you are in. ﴿Nor can you help me﴾ from what I am in. He mentioned this, although it was not within the realm of possibility, as an exaggeration in clarifying his inability to rescue them, and as an announcement that he too is afflicted with the same affliction they suffer, and in need of rescue. How then could he rescue others? For this reason he chose the nominal sentence, as though what preceded was his answer to their rebuke and reproach, and this is his answer to their pleas and their seeking his help in repelling the punishment that has overtaken them. It was also recited with a kasrah on the ya' (﴿مُصْرِخِيَّ﴾). ﴿Indeed, I disbelieve﴾ today ﴿in your associating me﴾ previously, meaning: in your associating me (with Allah). It means: I disavowed it and rejected it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association﴾. The meaning is: your associating me with Allah, glory be to Him, is what made you hope for my support for you, on the basis that you had a right over me, since you made me an object of worship, and I used to wish for that and desire it. Today, I have disbelieved in that, and I did not praise it, nor did I accept it from you. Rather, I disassociated myself from it and from you, so no bond remains between me and you. Or it means: I disbelieved previously, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, in the One you associated with me, who is Allah, Exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him who subjected these to us﴾. Thus this would be a rationale for his inability to rescue them, since one who disbelieves in Allah, glory be to Him, is far removed from giving aid and assistance, whether by repelling or by intercession. As for making it a rationale for their not calling on him for help, there is no basis for this, since there is no possibility of it that would need a rationale, and because giving disbelief as the cause of their not calling on him implies that they would have been in a position to do so were it not for an obstacle on his part. ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers will have a painful punishment﴾. This is either the completion of his speech, or the beginning of a statement from Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In relating such things there is gentleness for the listeners and an awakening for them, so that they will take account of themselves and reflect upon their outcomes.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 23:

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds will be admitted into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein by the permission of their Lord﴾ That is, by His command, or by His enabling (tawfiq) and guidance. In the mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to their pronoun, there is a display of further kindness toward them. And those who admit them are the angels, peace be upon them.

It has been read in the first-person form (wa-udkhilu), so that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿by the permission of their Lord﴾ is connected to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾. That is: the angels greet them with peace by the permission of their Lord.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 24:

﴿Have you not considered﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and it is connected with what follows it, the words of the Exalted: ﴿how Allah sets forth a parable﴾, meaning: how He adopted it and placed it in its fitting position.

﴿A good word﴾ is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb. That is: He made a good word, namely the word of tawhid (the declaration of God's oneness), or any good word such as tasbih (saying "Subhan Allah"), tahmid (saying "al-hamdu lillah"), istighfar (seeking forgiveness), tawbah (repentance), and da'wah (invitation to the faith).

﴿like a good tree﴾ means: He judged it to be like it, not that He made it like it in external reality. This is an explanation of His words "Allah sets forth a parable," as in your saying: "The emir honored Zayd: he clothed him in a robe and mounted him on a horse." It is also permissible for "a word" to be a substitute (badal) for "a parable," with "like a tree" being its description (sifah); or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is like a tree. It is also possible that it is the first of the two objects of "sets forth," treated as if it were "made" (ja'ala), with the second object delayed, namely "a parable," so that it does not become distant from its description, which is "like a tree." It has also been read in the nominative, as a beginning (mubtada').

﴿Its root is firm﴾ means: it is driving its roots into the earth. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) recited: "like a good tree, its root being firm" (thabit asluha). The reading of the majority is stronger in its composition and more appropriate to its context, namely His words, ﴿and its branches﴾, meaning its top, ﴿are in the sky﴾, in the direction of height. It is also permissible that "wa-furu'uha" be intended in the plural, the singular noun of the genus being sufficient in place of the plural.

(p-44) ﴿Tu'tī ukulahā﴾ (it gives its fruit) means it yields its produce, ﴿kulla ḥīn﴾ (every season), a time which God Most High set for its bearing fruit, ﴿bi-idhni rabbihā﴾ (by the permission of its Lord), by the will of its Creator. The intended meaning of "the tree" described is either the palm tree, as has been related in a report traced to the Prophet, or a tree in Paradise.

﴿Wa-yaḍribu Allāhu al-amthāla li-l-nāsi la'allahum yatadhakkarūn﴾ (And God strikes parables for the people, so that they may remember), because in striking them there is greater conveying of meaning and reminding. For it is a depiction of meanings through the forms of sensible things.

The Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 26:

﴿And the likeness of an evil word﴾ is the word of disbelief and the call to it, or the denial of the truth, or what encompasses all of these, or every ugly word.

﴿Like an evil tree﴾ i.e., like the likeness of an evil tree. It has been said: it is every tree whose fruit is not good, such as the colocynth (ḥanẓal), the dodder (kashūth), and the like. The change of style (from a direct comparison to the form "like an evil tree") serves to indicate that this is not the intended purpose of the parable and explanation; rather, it is an evident matter that everyone knows. ﴿Uprooted﴾: it was eradicated, and its trunk was entirely removed. ﴿From above the earth﴾: because its roots are near the surface. ﴿Having no stability﴾: no firmness upon it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 27:

﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word﴾ — the word that is firmly established by proof in their hearts and has taken root in their hearts. It is the good word whose remarkable attribute was mentioned, ﴿in the life of this world﴾, so they do not waver from it when they are tested in their religion, like Zakariyya, Yahya, Jirjis, Shamsun, and those whom the People of the Trench (Ashab al-Ukhdud) tormented. ﴿And in the Hereafter﴾, so they do not falter when they are asked about their belief at the place of standing (al-mawqif), nor are they overwhelmed by the terrors of the Resurrection, or at the questioning in the grave.

It is related that he (ﷺ) mentioned the taking of the soul of the believer and said: "Then his soul is returned to his body, and two angels come to him and seat him in his grave, and they say: 'Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?' He says: 'My Lord is Allah, my religion is Islam, and my Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ).' Then a caller calls out from the heaven: 'He has spoken truly, My servant.'" That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah keeps firm those who believe﴾.

This is an example of the tree mentioned giving its fruit every time. Al-Tha'labi said in his Tafsir: Abu al-Qasim ibn Habib informed me in the year 386 (AH), saying: I heard Abu al-Tayyib Muhammad ibn 'Ali al-Khayyat say: I heard Sahl ibn 'Ammar al-'Amali say: I saw Yazid ibn Harun in my dream after his death, and I said: "What did Allah do with you?" He said: "Two harsh angels came to me in my grave and said: 'Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?' So I took hold of my white beard and said to them: 'Is this said to someone like me, when I have taught people your answer for eighty years?' And they left."

﴿And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: He creates in them misguidance from the truth upon which He keeps the believers firm, according to their will and choice. The intended are the disbelievers, as is shown by what is contrasted with them. Describing them as wrongdoers is either by considering that they place a thing in other than its place, or by considering that they wronged themselves, since they changed the natural disposition (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created people, and so they were not guided to the firm word. Or, it applies to everyone who wrongs himself by limiting himself to blind imitation (taqlid) and turning away from clear proofs, so he does not stand firm at the times of trials and is not guided to the truth. Thus, "those who believe" in this case means those sincere in faith and firmly rooted in certainty, as indicated by the word "keeping firm." However, this may give the impression that the word of tawhid, if it is not from certainty, falls under what has no stability from the tree that was set forth as a parable.

﴿And Allah does what He wills﴾ of keeping some firm and misguiding others, as His will, which follows wise purposes, requires. The emphatic use of the noble Name in both places conveys great majesty and inspires awe, and also signals the difference in the source of keeping firm and of misguidance, for the source from which each proceeds from Him, glorified and exalted, is one of His supreme attributes, different from the source of the other.

**﴿Have you not seen﴾** is an expression of wonder, addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or to everyone, at what the disbelievers have fabricated of falsehoods, falsehoods that scarcely issue from anyone possessing even the slightest understanding. That is, "Have you not looked at **﴿those who exchanged the blessing of Allah﴾**," meaning the thankfulness for His blessing, Exalted is He, by placing disbelief in its position, **﴿disbelief﴾** great and a denial of it. Or it means they exchanged the very blessing for disbelief: when they disbelieved in it, it was taken from them, so they came to substitute disbelief for it, like the people of Makkah. Allah, glorified is He, created them, settled them in His secure sanctuary to which the fruits of every thing are brought, made them the custodians of His House, and honored them with Muhammad (ﷺ). But they disbelieved in that, so they were struck with drought for seven years, were killed, and were taken captive on the Day of Badr. Thus they became humiliated, deprived of the blessing, remaining in disbelief in its place.

It is related from Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they said: "They are the two wicked families of Quraysh: the Banu al-Mughira and the Banu Umayya. As for the Banu al-Mughira, you were sufficient against them on the Day of Badr. As for the Banu Umayya, they were given enjoyment for a time." It is as if the two of them were interpreting what will be recited of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: **﴿Say, "Enjoy yourselves"﴾** and the verse [continues].

**﴿And caused to alight﴾**, that is, they settled **﴿their people﴾** by guiding them to the way of polytheism and misguidance, and the non-mention of their alighting is indicated by the word "caused to alight," since it is a branch of alighting, as in His saying, Exalted is He: **﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection and bring them down into the Fire﴾**.

**﴿The abode of destruction﴾**, the abode of ruin, beyond which there is no ruin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 29:

﴿Jahannam﴾ is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it. In the vagueness and then the clarification there is an evident intensification of the terror (al-tahwil), which needs no elaboration.

﴿Yaslawnaha﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to it [Jahannam], or to their people (qawmihim), meaning: entering into it, enduring its heat. Or it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the manner of the alighting. Or it is an explanatory verb (mufassir) for a verb that is presumed to govern Jahannam as its object. The intended meaning of the mentioned "alighting" then is: exposing them to destruction by killing and capture. However, the words of the Exalted, ﴿Say: enjoy yourselves, for your destiny is indeed the Fire﴾, are more fitting to the first interpretation. ﴿And wretched is the abode (al-qarar)﴾ has its object of blame omitted, meaning: wretched is the dwelling place, Jahannam; or: wretched is the abode, their abode therein. In it is the implication that their alighting and their burning are in a manner of perpetuity and continuance.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 14, verse 30:

﴿And they set up﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "they caused to alight" (aḥallū), and what is conjoined to it is included together with both within the scope of the relative clause (ṣila) and the ruling of wonder (taʿjīb). That is: they set up in their belief and judgment, ﴿for God﴾, the One, the Eternal Refuge, "there is nothing like unto Him" (Qur'an 42:11), who is the One, the Subduer.

﴿Rivals﴾: equals in worship. ﴿That they might lead astray﴾ their people, who follow them, just as they themselves went astray, ﴿from His way﴾, the upright one, which is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and throw them into the pit of disbelief and error. Perhaps the change of order, although the apparent sequence of the text would require that their ingratitude for God's blessing be mentioned first, then their disbelief in His very Essence, exalted is He, by taking rivals, and then their leading their people astray, which leads to their settling them in the abode of perdition, is for the sake of doubling the wonder and repeating it, and to signal that each of these three matters, namely placing disbelief in the place of gratitude, causing their people to settle in the abode of perdition, and taking rivals in order to mislead, is a matter from which wonder is due. Had the text been arranged in the order of occurrence, the wonder might have been understood only from the combined totality of the three blunders, as in the story of the cow. It is also read: (liyaḍillū) with a fatḥa [i.e., "that they might go astray"] (p-46). Whatever the reading, that is not a true purpose for them in taking rivals; but since it was a result of it, it was likened to a purpose and the lam was introduced upon it by way of subsequent metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya).

﴿Say﴾: as a threat to those misguided misleaders, a rebuke against them, and a signal that, because of the intensity of their refusal to accept the truth, their excessive immersion in falsehood, and their failure to desist from that in any way, they are worthy that one turn away from them, withdraw the reins of admonition from them, leave them to their own affairs, and not be forbidden from it, but rather be commanded to engage in it, as an exaggeration of abandonment and forsaking, and as a hastening to make clear its disastrous consequence. It is said to them: ﴿Enjoy yourselves﴾ in what you are upon of appetites, among which is the ingratitude for great blessings, and leading people into the worship of idols.

﴿For indeed your destiny is the Fire﴾, nothing else. So there is no escape for you from pursuing what necessitates that and what your conditions require of it. Rather, in reality, this is a depiction of its entry and an example of it, as is hinted at by His words, glorified is He: ﴿and they caused their people to alight in the abode of perdition﴾ ... etc., so it is a justification for the command given, and in it is severe threat and firm warning, beyond description. Or say to them, as a depiction of their state and an expression of what compels them to that: "Enjoy yourselves," signaling that, because of their extreme immersion in the enjoyment of what they are in, without any restraint turning them aside or any inclination turning them back, they are commanded to do so by the one who commands desire, submitting to its judgment and obeying its order, like the habit of a commanded servant striving in the service of an obeyed master. Thus His words, exalted is He, "for indeed your destiny is the Fire," are then not a justification for the command, but rather the answer to a conditional clause implied by the speech, as if it were said: "This is your state; if you remain upon it, then indeed your destiny is the Fire." In this lies the threat and the warning, not in the command.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 31:**

﴿Say to My servants who have believed﴾: He singled them out by attributing them to Himself, to honour them and to draw attention to the fact that they are the ones who uphold the duties of servitude (*'ubudiyyah*) and fulfil its rights. The conjunction is omitted between the two imperatives to indicate that their situations differ, given the one being addressed, in terms of threat and honour. The verb of saying (*al-maqul*) is elided here, and the response (*al-jawab*) indicates it, meaning: say to them, "Establish," and "spend," ﴿that they establish the prayer and spend from what We have provided them﴾, that is, that they persist in that. In this there is an indication of their complete obedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) and their utmost haste in complying with his commands. It has also been permitted that the elided verb of saying be "establish" and "spend," with the imperative particle (*lam al-amr*, the lam of command) deleted from both. This is acceptable there, but not with the deletion in the verse of the poet:

*Muhammad, let every soul be ransom for you, if you fear any calamity*

because of the indication of "say" (*qul*) in it.
