It has been said that both are the answers (*jawab*) of "establish" and "spend," which have been placed in their stead, but this is not the case. ﴿Secretly and openly﴾ are both in the accusative as verbal nouns (*masdar*) of the implied imperative, not as the response of the stated imperative; that is, "spend the spending of secrecy and openness." The more preferred practice in spending is to conceal voluntary charity and to make obligatory charity public. The purpose is to urge the believers to thank God, glorified is He, for His blessings, through bodily and financial worship, and through abandoning enjoyment of the goods of this world and inclining toward them, as is the practice of disbelief.

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trading﴾, so that the one who fell short may buy what makes up for his shortfall, or ransom himself with it. The intended meaning is the total negation of the contract of exchange. Trading is singled out for mention for conciseness together with emphasis on negating the contract, since the absence of trading, which entails the absence of buying, is in the most eloquent form, and its absence is conceivable alongside the existence of an offer from the seller. ﴿Nor friendship﴾, nor companionship, so that a friend may intercede for him, or so that someone may forgive him with money by which he ransoms himself. Alternatively, it means: before there comes a Day in which there is no effect of what they used to busy themselves with, namely trading and friendship (*al-mukhallah*), and no benefit from that. Benefit and advantage in that Day come only through spending for the sake of God, glorified is He.

It is apparent that "from" (*min*) is connected to "spend." The mention of the coming of that Day is to reinforce its content, as in Surat al-Baqarah. This is because each of the absence of intercession and the absence of what might make up for shortfall, whether by exchange or by gift, and the cessation of the effects of trading and friendship, which exist in this world, together with the failure to benefit from them, are among the strongest motives for performing that whose benefits remain and whose advantages endure, namely spending in the way of God, mighty and majestic is He. Or it means that the storing of wealth and the refraining from spending it generally occurs for the sake of trade and gifting; so, since that is impossible in the Hereafter, there is no reason to store wealth until the time of death. The emphasis is specified with this because of the inclination of natures toward wealth, their being created to love it and to be stingy with it. It is not far-fetched that it is also an emphasis on the content of the command to establish the prayer, since neglecting it often happens through being occupied with sales and friendships, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it﴾.

It has also been read with a *fath* (the vowel *fatha*) on both words (*bay'un* and *khilalun*), on the intention of general negation, and the indication of the *raf'* (nominative) to that is by a rhetorical consideration, namely its occurring in the answer to the question: "Is there trading in it, or friendship?"

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 32:**

﴿Allah﴾ is a *mubtada'* (subject of a nominal sentence), and its *khabar* (predicate) is ﴿who created the heavens﴾, including what is in them of the celestial bodies, ﴿and the earth﴾, including what is in it of the kinds of created things. When He mentioned the states of the disbelievers regarding the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, and commanded the believers to establish the forms of obedience in gratitude for His blessings, He began to detail what necessitates on all of mankind persistence in gratitude and obedience, from among the great blessings and mighty favours, as an incitement to the believers to them, and as a rebuke to the disbelievers who neglect them and put disbelief and sins in their place. In making the subject the sublime Name and the predicate the relative pronoun with those great acts, namely the creation of these great celestial bodies, the sending down of rain, the bringing forth of fruits, and the wondrous effects that follow them, there is evident the cultivation of awe and an indication of the power of the sovereignty.

﴿And sent down from the sky﴾, i.e., from the clouds. For everything above you is called "sky," or from the sphere, and the rain begins from it, rising to the clouds and from there down to the earth, according to what the apparent texts indicate. Or [it comes] from heavenly causes which stir the moist particles from the depths of the earth into the atmosphere, where they condense into rain-bearing clouds. In either case, ﴿min﴾ (من) is *ibtida'iyyah* (indicating the starting point).

﴿water﴾, i.e., a kind of it, which is rain. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the object, either by considering it the starting point of its descent, or for its honour, as in your saying: "The sultan gave him money from his treasury," or because of the suspense toward the postponed element, as has repeatedly been mentioned. ﴿Then brought forth thereby﴾, by that water, ﴿fruits﴾ [using the plural form] ... [The use of the] ﴿min﴾ [in ﴿mina al-thamarat﴾] is for partitive division [*li-l-ta'bid*] ... either because the plural forms are interchangeable with one another, or because by its singular is intended the collective of "fruit" found in your saying: "The fruit of so-and-so's orchard has ripened."

﴿Provision for you﴾, by which you live. It has the meaning of "what is provided," and includes what is eaten and what is worn, as an object of *akhraja*. The *min* here is *li-l-tabyin* (explanatory), like your saying: "I spent a thousand of the dirhams." It is permissible that ﴿min al-thamarat﴾ be the object and ﴿rizqan﴾ a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from it, or a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *akhraja* in the sense of *razaqa*. Or the *min* may be *li-l-tab'id* (partitive), based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits﴾, as if it were said: He sent down from the sky some of the water, and by it brought forth some of the fruits, so that they might be some of your provision. For He did not send down all the water from the sky, nor bring forth with the rain all the fruits, nor make all provision fruit. The bringing forth of fruits, although it is by His will, may He be glorified and exalted, and His power, nevertheless His customary practice, exalted is He, has been to join their forms and modes to the materials mixed from water and earth, or He has deposited in water an active power and in earth a receptive power, from whose union the kinds of fruits are generated. He is capable of bringing things into existence without causes and materials, just as He originated the essences of causes. Likewise, for Him, exalted is He, in their creation there is a gradual progression from stage to stage, works, and wisdoms in which He renews for those of insight lessons and tranquillity in the greatness of His power, which would not be present if they were originated all at once. His saying ﴿for you﴾ is an attribute of ﴿provision﴾ if by it is meant the thing provided, and an object (*maf'ul bihi*) if by it is meant the verbal noun, as if it were said: "Provision: [for] you."

﴿And He subjected for you the ships﴾, by enabling you to build them and to use them, by inspiring in you the manner of doing so, ﴿so that they run in the sea﴾, running that follows your will, ﴿by His command﴾, by His will, to which everything is attached. The specifying of this by mention is to make explicit that this is not by the mere practice of works and the use of instruments, as appears from the outward situation. ﴿And He subjected for you the rivers﴾. If by them is meant the great waters flowing in the large rivers, as the mention of them beside the sea indicates, then their subjection is making them prepared for the benefit of people, in that they take from them channels by which they irrigate their crops, their gardens, and the like. If by them is meant the rivers themselves, then their subjection is making them easy for them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 33:

﴿And He subjected for you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses﴾ — they persist in their motion and in their giving light, perpetually and in succession, and in their setting right of what is bound to their soundness among created beings. ﴿And He subjected for you the night and the day﴾ — they succeed one another in alternation, for your sleep, your livelihood, and for the ripening and the setting of fruits and their maturing. Glorified and exalted is He, He mentioned the kinds of blessings that overflow upon them, and He set forth each one of them in an independent clause, to draw attention to its importance, to alert to the lofty rank of its place, and to make explicit that each of them is a magnificent blessing deserving of gratitude. In expressing the disposal related to what has been mentioned — the ship, the rivers, the sun, the moon, the night and the day — by the word "subjection" (taskhir), there is an indication, which is not hidden, of the difficulty of its grasp, the rarity of its attainment, and a demonstration of the greatness of the sovereignty and the intensity of the impossibility (of its being otherwise). The postponement of the subjection of the sun and the moon from the subjection of the things mentioned before them among the enumerated matters, together with the apparent connection between it and the creation of the heavens, is due to the fact that mentioning them leads on to the mention of the earth, which calls for mention of the sending down of water from it to it, which necessitates mention of the bringing forth of provision, part of which is what is obtained through the ship and the rivers. Or it is to guard against the assumption that all of it — I mean the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the subjection of the sun and the moon — is a single blessing, as has passed in the story of the Cow (al-Baqarah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 34:

﴿And He gave you of all that you asked of Him.﴾ That is: He gave you some part of the whole of what you asked of Him, as His will, which follows wisdom and benefit, requires. Like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Whoever desires the hastening (world), We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire.﴾ Or: He gave you of all that, what you needed, and upon which the good ordering of your affairs in the determined manner depends, so it is as if you had asked for it. Or: all that you sought through the tongue of readiness (istidad). Or: all that you asked for, with "min" being explanatory (lil-bayan), and the word "kull" being for amplification (lil-taksir), as when you say: "So-and-so knows everything," and "All the people came to him." And upon this is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿We opened for them the gates of every thing.﴾ It has also been said: the original is "He gave you of all that you asked of Him, and what you did not ask," and the second part was omitted because what remained indicates what was omitted. It has also been read with "kull" tanwin (kullin), with "ma" being negative, and the place of "ma sa'altumuhu" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He gave you of every (thing) without your asking for it.

﴿And if you count the blessing of Allah﴾ which He has bestowed upon you, ﴿you cannot enumerate it﴾, you cannot manage to count it, even in summary, for it is endless. The origin of ihsa' (enumeration) is that the reckoner, when he reaches a specific group of numbers, places a pebble so that he may keep count by it. In this there is an announcement that one cannot reach a level worth counting among its levels, let alone reach its end. How could it be otherwise? For there is no single individual among people, even if he is in the furthest degree of poverty and destitution, who is not endowed with kinds of care and tested with types of calamities; rather, if you contemplate him you will find him turning in blessings without limit and favours that cannot be counted or numbered. It is as if he has been given, at every hour and moment, of the bounties what the scope of possibility encompasses. And if you are in doubt about this, then suppose a king ruled the regions of the world, and all the nations submitted to him, and the nobles yielded to his obedience, and the necks of the tyrants bowed before his awe, and he attained every aim, obtained every gain, and possessed all that is in the world of kinds of wealth, without any rival contending with him or any partner sharing with him; rather, suppose that all that is in it of stone and clay were precious rubies and rare pearls. Then suppose that he has lost a drink or a food, in a state where his soul has reached the throat. Would he, in that state, buy with all his wealth of kingdom and property a morsel that saves him from his suffocation, or a sip that quenches his thirst? Or would he choose death, so that the wealth and the possessions go away without any substitute remaining for him and without any benefit returning to him? No indeed; rather he would give for that all that his two hands hold, whatever it may be, and there is no loss in his transaction. Then that morsel and that sip are better than what is in the world by a thousandfold, although they are within reach, which he can obtain whenever he wills, of nights and days. Or suppose that the breath has been held back from him, so that nothing enters from him that goes out, and nothing goes out from him that enters. The appointed time has come, and death has come upon him from every place. Would he give all that for the exchange of one breath? Rather, he would give it while he is praising his opinion. Then he is better than the wealth of the world with all its carrying and all its demands in their entirety, although it is permitted to him at every moment of the nights and days, in wakefulness and in sleep. This is so evident and clear that it is hardly hidden from anyone among the intelligent. And if you seek to reach the reality of the truth, and to stand upon everything of the secret that is grand and subtle, know that the human being, by the requirement of his possible reality, is far removed from deserving existence, and from what follows it of fitting perfections and pleasing qualities. So if the connection between him and divine care were severed, he would never find settlement, nor would he be at rest in the abode, except in the pit of non-existence and ruin, and the abysses of destruction and perdition. But there overflows upon him from the Most Holy Presence, exalted is His station and sanctified, at every time that passes and every moment that goes by and ends, kinds of overflowing bounties connected with His essence, His existence, and all His spiritual, soulish, and bodily attributes, which the scope of expression cannot encompass, and which none knows except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. Its clarification: just as he does not deserve existence at the beginning, so he does not deserve it in continuance; rather, that comes from the Source of Origination, mighty and majestic is He. Thus, just as his existence cannot be conceived at the beginning unless all the modes of his original non-existence are closed to him, so his remaining in existence after its realization by its cause cannot be conceived unless all the modes of his incidental non-existence are closed to him, because continuance and permanence are among the properties of necessary existence. You know well that what his existence depends upon, of existential matters which are its causes and conditions, though it is necessary that they be finite, since whatever falls under existence must be finite, nevertheless the non-existential matters which have a role in his existence are not like that, for there is no impossibility that a single thing have endless impediments; the impossibility lies only in their entering under existence. Thus the removal of those impediments, which are endless, I mean their remaining in non-existence while their existence is possible in themselves at every moment of his existence, are endless blessings in reality, not merely by claim. The same holds for the existences of his causes and conditions, near and far, at the beginning and in continuance, and likewise for his perfections which follow his existence. It becomes clear, then, that there overflows upon him at every moment endless blessings from many aspects. So glory be to You, glory be to You; how great is Your dominion. The eyes do not perceive You with their glances, and the intellects do not comprehend You with their thoughts. Your state is not matched, and Your beneficence has no end. We are bewildered in knowing You, and deficient in performing the rites of thanking You. We ask You for guidance to the paths of knowing You, and for success in fulfilling the rights of Your blessing. We cannot count the praise of You. There is no god but You. We seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance.

﴿Indeed, the human being is surely a wrongdoer﴾, who wrongs the blessing by neglecting its thanks, or by placing it in other than its proper place, or who wrongs himself by exposing himself to deprivation, ﴿a great ingrate﴾, exceedingly ungrateful. It has been said: he is a wrongdoer in hardship, he complains and panics; an ingrate in blessing, he accumulates and withholds. The "al" in "al-insan" is for the genus, and the instance of the judgment of wrongdoing and ingratitude is some of those individuals in whom both are found; and within this enter, as a first entry, those who ﴿exchanged the blessing of Allah for disbelief﴾, and so on.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 35:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ — i.e., remember the time when he, peace be upon him, said it. The purpose of this reminder is to recall, in detail, the statements that were made by him, peace be upon him, and the intention behind it is to confirm what preceded regarding his, peace be upon him, marvelling at their (the Quraysh's) misdeeds, by presenting another kind of their crimes: they disbelieved in the blessings specific to them after they had disbelieved in the general blessings, and they disobeyed their father Abraham, peace be upon him, when he settled them in Makkah, may Allah exalt it, so that they would establish the prayer, abstain from worshipping idols, and be thankful for the blessings of Allah, the Exalted. He asked Allah, the Exalted, to make it a secure land, to provide them with fruits, and to make the hearts of people incline towards them from every deep ravine. So Allah, the Exalted, answered his supplication and made it a sanctuary secure, to which the fruits of everything are brought. Yet they disbelieved in those great blessings, exchanged the Sacred Land for the abode of perdition, set up rivals to Allah, and did what they did. ﴿My Lord, make this land﴾ — meaning Makkah, may Allah the Glorified exalt it — ﴿secure﴾, i.e., possessing security, or its people being secure, such that fear is not experienced in it, as has passed in Surat al-Baqarah. The difference between this and what is there in His saying: ﴿My Lord, make this a secure land﴾ is that what was requested there was both the (quality of being a) land (bala­diyyah, i.e., being a city/settled territory) and security together, whereas here it is security alone, since it has been made the second object of the verb "make," and "land" has been made a qualifier of the first object.

If it is understood as a multiplicity of requests, then perhaps he, peace be upon him, first asked for both matters and was granted one of them, while the other was delayed until its appointed time, according to the wisdom that requires it, and then he repeated the request, as is customary in supplication and entreaty. Or the first request was merely for security sufficient to make residence possible, as in all other lands, and this was granted to him; and the second was the specific security. Or both were requested in each case, and both were granted as well, but the second request was for permanence and for restriction to that alone, because it is the original intent, or because it is customary for the quality of being a settled land to continue after it has been established, unlike security. If it is understood as a single request with the account repeated, as is most apparent, then the apparent meaning is that both matters were requested, and the one was reported first; here he confined the report to the request for security, not merely because the blessing of security is more deserving of gratitude, so that mentioning it is more fitting to the context of rebuking the disbelievers for neglecting it, as has been said. Rather, it is because the request for settled-land status has been reported by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So make hearts from among the people incline towards them﴾, since what was requested is that they be drawn towards them in order to dwell with them, not for Hajj alone. This is the very same request reported in another expression. This was the first thing he, peace be upon him, did upon arriving in Makkah, as Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: that when he, peace be upon him (p-51), settled Isma'il and Hajar there and returned, heading towards Syria, Hajar followed him and began saying: "To whom are you leaving us in this barren valley?" He would not answer her, until she said: "Has Allah commanded you to do this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then He will not neglect us," and she was content, and he went on until, when he reached the ridge of Kada', he turned towards the valley and said: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring﴾ — the verse. The two matters were detailed separately only for the sake of emphasis on the favour, and to announce that each of them is a magnificent blessing entailing much gratitude, as in the story in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿And keep me and my sons﴾ — distance me and them ﴿from worshipping idols﴾ — and place us in a far side from them, i.e., keep us steadfast upon what we were upon of monotheism, the religion of Islam, and distance from the worship of idols. It is read (wa-ajnibni) from the form of if'al, and both are the dialect of the people of Najd, who say: "Jannibni sharrahu" and "Ajnibni sharrahu"; whereas the people of the Hijaz say: "Jannibni sharrahu." In this there is evidence that the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, is by the grace of Allah, the Exalted. The apparent meaning is that by "his sons" is meant his biological descendants. Thus there is no argument in it for Ibn 'Uyaynah, may Allah be pleased with him, that none of Isma'il's descendants worshipped an idol; rather, each people had a stone which they erected and said, "It is a stone, and the House is a stone," so they would circumambulate it and call it "the Circler," and so it was preferred to say "tawaf (circumambulated) the House" and not "dara (circled) around the House." I wonder how this escaped him, given the admonitions in the Noble Qur'an that censure the Quraysh for worshipping idols; moreover, what he mentioned is a reversion upon what he fled from.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 36:

﴿My Lord, indeed they have led many of the people astray.﴾ That is, the idols (aṣnām) ﴿have led many of the people astray﴾; that is, they have been the cause of it. It is like His saying, exalted is He: "and the life of this world has deceived them" [cf. 6:70]. This is a justification for his supplication. He began it with the vocative (nidā') only to show his concern for it (iʿtināʾ) and his eagerness for it to be answered.

﴿So whoever follows me﴾ from among them in what I call to of tawḥīd (the affirmation of God's oneness) and the creed (milla) of Islam, ﴿then he is of me﴾; that is, part of me. He (peace be upon him) said this to emphasize the closeness of that person to him, or [it means] he is connected to me and is never separated from me in matters of religion.

﴿And whoever disobeys me﴾; that is, does not follow me. The expression of this by "disobedience" (iṣyān) is to indicate that he (peace be upon him) was persistent in the call, and that the non-following of one who did not follow him is only because of his disobedience, not because the call had not reached him.

﴿Indeed You are Forgiving, Merciful﴾; able to forgive him and show mercy to him from the outset, or after his repentance. In this is [the indication] that every sin is something God, exalted is He, may forgive, even shirk, except that the threat (wa'īd) has decreed a distinction between it and other [sins].

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 37:**

﴿Our Lord﴾: He (peace be upon him) used the plural pronoun, not because of what was said about the previous mention of himself and his sons, for otherwise he would have observed it in his words "My Lord, they have indeed led astray many of the people" and so on. Rather, it is because the supplication that opens with it, and what he presents as a preface to the acceptance of his prayer, from his words "I have settled" to the end of the verse, relates to his descendants. Therefore, mentioning the attribute of His lordship (rubbubiyyah) toward them is more conducive to acceptance and to the granting of the request.

﴿Some of my descendants (dhurriyyah)﴾: that is, some of them, or a group from my descendants. The object is omitted, and it is Isma'il (peace be upon him) and what will be born to him. For settling him, given that it was in a manner of tranquility, implies settling them as well. It is narrated that Hajar, the mother of Isma'il (peace be upon him), belonged to Sarah, who gave her to Ibrahim (peace be upon him). When she bore Isma'il (peace be upon him) to him, Sarah became jealous of them both and implored him to remove them from her presence. So he took them out to the land of Makkah, and Allah, exalted is He, caused the spring of Zamzam to appear.

﴿In an uncultivated valley﴾: a valley in which there is no cultivation at all, and it is the valley of Makkah, may Allah, exalted is He, honor it. ﴿By Your Sacred House﴾: this is an adverbial complement (zarf) of "I have settled," like your saying, "I prayed in Makkah by the Corner." It is not that it is a qualifier (sifah) of "valley," or a substitute (badal) for it. The intent is to show that this settlement, despite the absence of its prerequisites, was purely for the sake of drawing near to Allah, exalted is He, and seeking refuge in His noble protection, as the mention of the title of sanctity (hurmah), which indicates the might of the one sought for refuge and his safety from harm, indicates in His words, exalted is He: ﴿the Sacred﴾, where its violation and its disrespect are forbidden. Or it has never ceased to be venerated and protected, one whom tyrants have feared in every age. Or the flood was prevented from it, so it did not overpower it, and for this reason it was called "ancient" (ʿatiq). Its being called a "house" at that time, when there was no structure, but it was only an elevated mound, like a hill that the torrents reach, so they divert to the right and to the left, is not by consideration of what its affair would eventually become after the building by him (peace be upon him). For that inclines toward considering the title of sanctity as well. Rather, it is by consideration of what existed before. For the multiple constructions of the venerated Ka'bah are beyond doubt, and the disagreement is only about the number of times it was built. We have mentioned this in surah al-Baqarah, by the grace of Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Our Lord, so that they may establish prayer﴾: turning toward Him and seeking blessing through Him. This is related to "I have settled." The specific mention of prayer among all the rites of the religion is because of its excellence, and the repetition of the address and its placement in the middle serve to show complete concern for establishing prayer and attention to presenting that the purpose of settling them in that barren valley is that ultimate goal and highest aim. All of this is to prepare the prerequisites for the acceptance of his supplication and the granting of his request, which this aim cannot be achieved without. For this reason the particle "fa" (so) is attached to it, when he says:

﴿So make hearts among people incline towards them﴾: that is, make hearts from among their hearts incline toward them. Thus "min" (from) is partitive (tab'id). For this reason it was said: if he had said "hearts of the people," Persia and the Romans would have crowded upon them. As for what has been added to it, namely the saying: "the Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage," it is not suitable to the context, since what is requested is directing hearts toward them for dwelling with them, not directing them to the House for pilgrimage. Otherwise it would have been said "they would yearn toward it," for that is the very content of the supplication for its being a city (al-baladiyyah), and it has been expressed in another phrasing, as has passed. Or "min" is for the beginning of the end (ibtida' al-ghayah), like your saying, "The heart from me is ill," meaning "the hearts of people." It was also recited as "ā'fidah" with the hamzah on the heart (qira'ah), like "ādar" in "adw'ur." Or it is an active participle from "afidat al-rihlah," meaning "the journey hastened," that is: a group of people. And "afidah," with the hamzah dropped from "al-af'idah," or as an epithet from "afid."

﴿Incline towards them﴾: hasten toward them in longing and affection. It was also recited with the passive form from "ahwāhu ghayruh" (another made him love it), and "tahwī" from the pattern of "ʿalima," meaning: they love. Its transitivity with "ilā" is because it includes the meaning of longing and yearning. The first effect of this supplication is what is narrated: a company from Jurhum passed by, wanting to go to Syria, and they saw birds circling over the mountain. They said, "This bird must be hovering over water," so they approached and found Hajar. They said to her, "If you wish, we will be with you, keep you company, and the water will be yours." So she permitted them, and they stayed with her until Isma'il (peace be upon him) grew up. Hajar died, and Isma'il married one of them, as is well known.

﴿And provide them﴾: that is, my descendants whom I have settled there, or along with whoever joins them from among the people. He did not restrict the supplication to the believers among them, as in His words, "And provide its people with fruits, those among them who believe in Allah and the Last Day," being content with the mention of establishing prayer.

﴿With fruits﴾: of their varieties, either by making villages near it where such things are produced, or by having them brought to it from distant regions. Both have occurred, to the extent that the fruits of spring, summer, and autumn gather there in a single day. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that al-Ta'if was from the land of Palestine. When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) made this supplication, Allah, exalted is He, lifted it and placed it where He placed it, as provision for the Sacred Sanctuary (al-Haram). And it is narrated from al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with him, that He, exalted is He, moved a village from the villages of Syria and placed it at al-Ta'if, in answer to the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

﴿So that they may be grateful﴾: for that blessing by establishing prayer and performing all the rites of worship. It was also said that the "lam" in "li-yuqimu" is the imperative lam (lam al-amr). The meaning would be: commanding them to establish prayer, and supplicating to Allah, exalted is He, that He grant them success in it. The "fa" in His words, exalted is He, "So make..." does not fit this. In his supplication (peace be upon him) there is observance of good manners, of the rules of humble entreaty, presenting the need, drawing down mercy, and soliciting compassion, which are not hidden. For by mentioning that the valley is uncultivated, he showed the extent of their need for the One being asked, and by mentioning that their settlement is by the Sacred House, he indicated that the neighborhood of the Generous One demands the bestowal of blessings. And by presenting that this settlement, despite the complete lack of means of livelihood, is purely for establishing prayer and fulfilling the rights of the House, he prepared all the prerequisites for the granting of the request. For this reason his supplication (peace be upon him) was joined with good acceptance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 38:

﴿Our Lord, You know what we conceal and what we disclose﴾ of needs and other things. What is meant by "what we conceal" is what stands opposite to "what we disclose," whether or not concealment applies to it. That is: You know what we manifest and what we do not manifest, for His knowledge, exalted is He, relates to what occurs to the mind of the heart of hidden states, let alone what is concealed. The placing of "what we conceal" before "what we disclose" serves to establish equality between the two in the relation of knowledge to them, in the most eloquent manner, as if His relation to what is hidden is older than His relation to what is disclosed. Or, because the rank of secrecy and hiddenness precedes the rank of openness, since nothing is disclosed except that it was hidden before that; thus the relation of His knowledge, glorified is He, to its first state is older than its relation to its second state. And the intent of his peace is that the manifestation of these needs, and what is from their beginnings and completions, is not because they are unknown to You, but rather it is for the manifestation of servitude, humility before Your greatness, submission to Your might, presentation of need for what is with You, haste to attain Your bounties, and the repetition of the call for the sake of intensifying supplication and entreaty. The pronoun of the plural is used because what is meant is not merely His knowledge, exalted is He, of their secret and their open, but of all the hidden things of the dominion and the kingdom (malakut). He has verified this with His saying, by way of parenthetical insertion.

﴿Nothing is hidden from Allah of anything on the earth or in the heaven﴾ because He is the Knower by His essence. So there is no matter that falls under existence, whatever it may be, in any time of the times, except that its existence in its own reality is knowledge in relation to Him, glorified is He. And He said, "Nothing is hidden from Allah..." etc., rather than saying, "and He knows what is in the heavens and the earth," to verify what He meant by His saying, "You know what we conceal," that His knowledge, exalted is He, of that is not in a manner in which there is any trace of hiddenness in relation to His knowledge, exalted is He, as that would be in relation to the knowledge of created beings. The word "fi" (in) relates to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of "shay'" (thing), meaning: a thing existing in them both, more general than whether that is in the manner of being fixed in them, or in the manner of being a part of them, or with "yakhfa" (is hidden). The placing of "al-ard" (the earth) before "al-sama'" (the heaven), with "la" inserted between them, is in consideration of nearness and distance from us, which call for difference in relation to our knowledge. The turn from address to the name of the Essence that comprises the attributes serves to cultivate awe and to indicate the cause of the judgment, in the manner of His exalted saying: ﴿Does He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the Aware﴾ [67:14], and to announce its generality, since it is not a matter specific to any particular thing or to whoever is related to it, but encompasses all things; so the fitting mention is of Him, exalted is He, under a title that validates the origin of the whole. It has been said: it is from the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, coming by way of parenthetical insertion to affirm His peace upon him, like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And thus they do﴾ [27:34]. And "min" is for generalization on both aspects.

﴿All praise is due to God, who granted me, in spite of old age﴾: that is, despite my old age and my despair of having a child. He restricted the gift by this, to magnify the blessing and to show gratitude for it.

﴿Isma'il and Ishaq﴾. It is narrated that Isma'il was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old, or one hundred and seventeen years old.

﴿Indeed my Lord﴾, the Master of my affair, ﴿is All-Hearing of supplication﴾, that is, the one who answers it. This is from the people's saying, "the king heard his speech," meaning he took it into account. *Samee'* (All-Hearing) is one of the intensive forms (*mubalagha*, emphatic patterns) that operate as a verb, with what follows it either annexed to its object, or to its subject, by attributing the hearing, figuratively (*majaz*), to God's answering of supplication. Although this is part of the praise and thanks, since it is a description of Him, Exalted be He, that this beautiful act is His constant practice, it serves as a causal explanation (*ta'lil*) in the manner of a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*) to the mentioned gift. In it is an indication of the multiplication of the blessing, since it came after the supplication, with his saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me of the righteous﴾, so the gift was joined with the acceptance of the prayer. The singular form of the speaker's pronoun is used, although it follows the mention of the gifting of both of them, because the blessing of the gift overflows upon him specifically, while they both are among the blessings, not among those who receive them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 40:

﴿My Lord, make me one who establishes the prayer﴾, persevering in it, maintaining it in its proper balance. The use of the singular first-person pronoun, even though his supplication extends also to his offspring, is because ﴿and from my offspring﴾ means: some of them, from among those mentioned, and whoever follows their way from among their children, to indicate that he (Abraham) is the one to be emulated in this, and that his offspring are his followers. He mentions them by way of digression (istitrad), not as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring﴾ ... etc. For his settling (of them) while it was not yet realized, without any connection to those he settled, is mentioned only as a preface (tamhid) to the supplication, which is specific to his offspring. He specified this supplication to some of his offspring because he knew, through God the Exalted, that some of them would not be ones who establish the prayer, as in the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, make us both submitting to You, and from our offspring a community submitting to You﴾. ﴿Our Lord, and accept my supplication﴾, that is, this my supplication of mine, concerning my being made, and the making of some of my offspring, establishers of the prayer, steadfast in that, avoiding the worship of idols. For this reason the plural pronoun was used.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 41:

﴿Our Lord, forgive me﴾, that is: for what has escaped from me of leaving the more excellent course (al-awla) in matters of religion, and other things that no human being is free from.

﴿and my parents﴾. It is also read as "and my parent" in the singular, and as "and my two parents" (liwalidayya or li-abawayya). This plea for forgiveness from him, peace be upon him, was only before the matter became clear to him, peace be upon him. It has been said that by his parents he meant Adam and Eve. It has also been said that it was conditional upon their being Muslims, but this is refuted by the words of the Most High: ﴿except the saying of Abraham﴾, and so on. A kind of investigation of this matter has already passed in surah al-Tawba, and its full treatment will come in surah Maryam, by the grace of God Most High.

﴿and the believers﴾ in general, from his descendants and others. To indicate that all of them share in the supplication for forgiveness, the plural pronoun was used.

﴿on the day when the reckoning takes place﴾, that is: the reckoning of the deeds of the responsible people, in accordance with justice, is established and realized. The expression is borrowed from the steadiness of one who stands firmly on his feet, and from it comes the idiom "the war stood on its leg" (qamat al-harb 'ala saq). The purpose is to convey its terror. It has been said that the standing is ascribed to the reckoning metaphorically (majaz), or that the omitted element is an elided genitive (mudaf mahdhuf), as in "ask the town" (wa-s'al al-qarya, Qur'an 12:82). Know that what is related from him, peace be upon him, of supplications and remembrances and what is connected with them, did not proceed from him in the order in which it is related, nor all together. Rather, it issued from him at various times, and it is narrated in sequence to show the bad condition of the disbelievers after his message became manifest in the religion, and to guide people to it, and to supplicate God Most High for their religious and worldly welfare.

﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware of what the wrongdoers do﴾. This is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The meaning is to affirm him in his state of not supposing that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is heedless, similar to His saying: ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾ and its like, together with what this implies of the absolute necessity of guarding against it, to the extent that it is forbidden to one who could not possibly engage in it. Or it is a prohibition to him, upon him be peace, from supposing that Allah, exalted is He, is heedless of them, leaving their punishment out of forgiveness. The expression of it in this way is for emphasis in the prohibition, and to indicate that such supposition is equivalent to supposing that Allah, exalted is He, is heedless of their deeds, since knowledge of them necessarily requires their punishment without doubt. Therefore, if He left them alone out of heedlessness of what their wicked deeds necessitate, this would be [the implication]. In it is consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a firm promise to him, and a severe threat to disbelievers and all wrongdoers. Or it is addressed to everyone who hastens their punishment, or who imagines that they are neglected, out of ignorance of the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, and being deceived by His granting them respite. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not suppose that He, exalted is He, treats them as one heedless of what they did, but rather as one who keeps account of their deeds and recompenses them for them, even for a speck or a trace. By "the wrongdoers" is meant the people of Makkah, whose evil deeds are enumerated, such as exchanging the blessing of Allah for disbelief, causing their people to alight in the abode of perdition, and taking rivals [to Allah]. As is indicated by the mention of the wisdom of the delay, which is announced by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: enjoy yourselves﴾, and so on. Or it refers to the category of wrongdoers, and they are included in the ruling by primary inclusion. ﴿He only delays them﴾, that is, gives them respite, letting them enjoy the worldly portions, and does not hasten their punishment, as is observed. This is a resumptive clause that comes as a reason for the preceding prohibition, meaning: continue in what you were upon, namely not supposing that Allah, exalted is He, is heedless of their deeds, and do not grieve over the delay of the painful punishment that they deserve, since the delay of it is for intensification and severity. Or: do not suppose that He, exalted is He, has abandoned their punishment because of what you see of its delay; it is only for this reason. Or: do not suppose that He, exalted is He, treats them as one heedless and does not take them to account for what they did because of the delay you see; it is only for this wisdom. It has been read with the nun [i.e., ﴿lā taḥsabanna﴾ with the nun being the emphatic ending]. The placing of the delay upon them, although what is delayed is their punishment, is to magnify the matter and depict the situation in its horror, by stating that they are headed toward punishment and kept in readiness for something, not that they remain by their own choice. It also indicates that their due portion of punishment is complete annihilation, leaving no trace or vestige of them in existence. And to announce that what is delayed is part of the punishment and its very title. Had it been said: "He only delays their punishment..." etc., this would not have been understood. ﴿For a Day﴾, terrifying, ﴿in which the eyes will stare﴾: the eyes of the people of the place of standing will be raised, so that the disbelievers in question enter among them by primary inclusion; that is, they will remain open, their eyelids not moving from the terror of what they see. Considering that they do not settle in their places is either by way of the sensory elevation in the substance of the eye, or by taking the form [of the verb] from one who departs from one town to another and travels in elevation.

﴿Muhtiʿīn﴾ (hastening): hurrying toward the one calling, coming toward him with fear, humility and submissiveness. Or: coming toward him with their eyes, not turning away from him, and not blinking out of awe and fear. Since the sustained gaze here is directed at the caller, it has been said: ﴿Muqniʿī ruʾūsihim﴾ (with their heads raised), meaning raising them while keeping their gaze fixed, without turning to anything else. This was said by al-ʿUtbī and Ibn ʿArafa. Or (it means) lowering them. It is said: aqnaʿa raʾsahu, meaning he lowered it and bowed it down. So it is one of the words with opposite meanings (ḍiddān), and both are circumstantial clauses (ḥāl) relating to what is indicated by "al-abṣār" (the eyes) from their owners. The second is a interlocking circumstantial clause (ḥāl mutadākhilah) from the pronoun in the first, and its attribution (iḍāfatuhu) is not literal, so it does not conflict with its being a circumstantial clause. ﴿Lā yartaddu ilayhim ṭarfuhum﴾ (their glance does not return to them): meaning the movement of their eyelids does not return to them as it used to every moment, but rather their eyes remain open and do not blink. Or, their eyelids, which are the instrument of the glance, do not return to them, so the attribution of returning to the glance is figurative (majāzī). Or it is the eyelid itself. Al-Fayrūzābādī said: al-ṭaraf is the eye, not pluralized, because it is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar), or it is a collective noun for the eye. Or their gaze does not return to themselves, let alone return to anything else (p-56) so they remain bewildered. This is also a circumstantial clause, or a substitute (badal) for "muqniʿī…" etc. Or it is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf), and the meaning is: what has come over them of the fixed staring of the eyes does not cease. Its placement (ta'khīruhu) away from what is part of its completion (of the hastening and raising of heads) is for the sake of cultivating this meaning, together with the connection between it and the mentioned fixed staring, which is appropriate.

﴿Wa-afʾidatuhum hawāʾ﴾ (and their hearts are hawāʾ): empty of understanding and comprehension, due to extreme bewilderment and astonishment, as if they were the very essence of air, empty of every preoccupation. From this, it is said of the coward and the fool: "his heart is hawāʾ," meaning he has no strength and no judgment in it. Considering their emptiness of all good does not suit the context. It is either a circumstantial clause whose governing element is "lā yartaddu," conveying that the fixed staring of their eyes and the non-return of their glance occur without understanding or choice. Or it is an independent sentence.

﴿وَأنْذِرِ النّاسَ﴾ [And warn mankind]: an address to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), after informing him of the reason for their delay, and a command to him to warn them and frighten them with it. By "mankind" is meant the disbelievers, who are described as "the wrongdoers," as the apparent sense of "the punishment coming to them" requires. The shift from the pronoun to this description indicates that the purpose of the warning is to restrain them from the wrongdoing they are engaged in, out of compassion for them, not to frighten them for the sake of distress and harm. Therefore it is appropriate not to mention them under the heading of wrongdoing. Or "mankind" means all people, since the warning is general to both groups, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنَّما تُنْذِرُ مَنِ اتَّبَعَ الذِّكْرَ﴾ [You can only warn those who follow the Reminder]. The coming (of the punishment) encompasses both groups insofar as both are in the place of standing, even though its reaching the disbelievers is specific to them. That is: warn them and frighten them.

﴿يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ العَذابُ﴾ [The Day the punishment comes to them]: "al-mahud" (the well-known day) is the day described with awe-inspiring attributes that cannot be fully described; namely, the Day of Resurrection. It has been said that it is the day of their death, while they are being tormented by the agonies of death and by meeting the angels without good tidings, or the day of their destruction by an immediate punishment. But the preceding restriction (qasr) rejects this view.

﴿فَيَقُولُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [then those who did wrong will say]: that is, fa-yaqulun (then they will say). The departure from this to what the noble composition has, namely the singular form, serves to record their wrongdoing against them and to indicate that the severity they encounter is only because of their wrongdoing. Preferring the form of the active participle (ẓālimīn) over the verb form, as mentioned at first, signifies that wrongdoing in general is sufficient to lead to the terrors mentioned, without needing to persist in it, as the form of the active participle indicates. On the assumption that by "mankind" is meant those who include the Muslims as well, the meaning is: those among them who did wrong, namely the disbelievers. Or every wrongdoer by associating partners with God and denying the truth, among those warned and among other earlier nations will say this, for the coming of the punishment encompasses them, as their promise to follow the messengers indicates.

﴿رَبَّنا أخِّرْنا﴾ [Our Lord, delay us]: return us to the world and grant us respite ﴿إلى أجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ﴾ [for a short term], to a period and limit of time that is near. ﴿نُجِبْ دَعْوَتَكَ﴾ [we will answer Your call]: that is, the call to You, meaning to Your Oneness, or Your call to us through the tongues of the messengers. In this there is a hint that they had acknowledged that the messengers were sent from God, exalted is He. ﴿وَنَتَّبِعِ الرُّسُلَ﴾ [and follow the messengers] in what they brought us. That is: we will make up for what we neglected of answering the call and following the messengers. The plural (the messengers) is either because all of them agreed upon the Oneness (of God), and their disobedience to the Messenger (ﷺ) is disobedience to all of them; or because what is related is the speech of the wrongdoers of all nations, and the intended meaning is to state the promise of each nation to follow its messenger.

﴿أوَلَمْ تَكُونُوا أقْسَمْتُمْ مِن قَبْلُ﴾ [Did you not swear before]: this is an implied verb of saying, coordinated with "fa-yaqulu" (then he says). That is: it will be said to them as a rebuke and reproach: "Were you not delayed in the world, and did you not swear at that time with your tongues, out of insolence, arrogance, ignorance and folly?"

﴿ما لَكم مِن زَوالٍ﴾ [that you would have no decline]: from what you are upon of enjoying worldly pleasures, or by the tongue of your state, since you built lofty buildings (mashid) and hoped for a far-off future, and did not tell yourselves that you would move from it to this condition. In this there is an indication of the lengthening of the period of delay and the distance of its extent. Or: that you would have no passing from this abode to another abode for requital. Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَأقْسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ جَهْدَ أيْمانِهِمْ لا يَبْعَثُ اللَّهُ مَن يَمُوتُ﴾ [And they swore by God their most emphatic oaths that God will not raise up those who die]. The form of address in the answer to the oath is to observe the state of address in "you swore," as in His saying: "He swore by God that he would certainly go out." It is more suited to rebuke than saying "what we have," which would observe the state of the one swearing. Al-Bayhaqi related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: The people of the Fire have five supplications, of which God, exalted is He, answers four. When the fifth comes, they will not speak after it forever. They say: ﴿رَبَّنا أمَتَّنا اثْنَتَيْنِ وأحْيَيْتَنا اثْنَتَيْنِ فاعْتَرَفْنا بِذُنُوبِنا فَهَلْ إلى خُرُوجٍ مِن سَبِيلٍ﴾ [Our Lord, You have made us die twice and given us life twice, and we have acknowledged our sins, so is there any way to get out?]. God, exalted is He, answers them: ﴿ذَلِكم بِأنَّهُ إذا دُعِيَ اللَّهُ وحْدَهُ كَفَرْتُمْ وإنْ يُشْرَكْ بِهِ تُؤْمِنُوا فالحُكْمُ لِلَّهِ العَلِيِّ الكَبِيرِ﴾ [That is because when God alone was invoked, you disbelieved, but when partners were associated with Him, you believed. So judgment belongs to God, the Most High, the Most Great]. Then they say: ﴿رَبَّنا أبْصَرْنا وسَمِعْنا فارْجِعْنا نَعْمَلْ صالِحًا إنّا مُوقِنُونَ﴾ [Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us, and we will do righteous deeds; indeed we are certain]. God, exalted is He, answers them: ﴿فَذُوقُوا بِما نَسِيتُمْ لِقاءَ يَوْمِكم هَذا﴾ [So taste (the punishment) because you forgot the meeting of this your Day]; the verse. Then they say: ﴿رَبَّنا أخِّرْنا إلى أجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ نُجِبْ دَعْوَتَكَ ونَتَّبِعِ الرُّسُلَ﴾ [Our Lord, delay us to a short term, we will answer Your call and follow the messengers]. God, exalted is He, answers them: ﴿أوَلَمْ تَكُونُوا أقْسَمْتُمْ﴾ [Did you not swear]; the verse. Then they say: ﴿رَبَّنا أخْرِجْنا نَعْمَلْ صالِحًا غَيْرَ الَّذِي كُنّا نَعْمَلُ﴾ [Our Lord, bring us out, we will do righteous deeds other than what we used to do]. God, exalted is He, answers them: ﴿أوَلَمْ نُعَمِّرْكم ما يَتَذَكَّرُ فِيهِ مَن تَذَكَّرَ وجاءَكُمُ النَّذِيرُ فَذُوقُوا فَما لِلظّالِمِينَ مَن نَصِيرٍ﴾ [Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would remember to remember, and the warner came to you? So taste (it), for the wrongdoers have no helper]. Then they say: "Our Lord, our wretchedness has overcome us, and we were a people astray." God, exalted is He, answers them: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me." So they do not speak after that forever; there is only groaning and wailing. At that point their hope was cut off, and some of them began to bark in each other's faces, and Hell enclosed them. O God, we seek refuge in You, and we take shelter in Your protection; Your protection is mighty, Your praise is exalted, and there is no god but You.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 45:**

﴿And you dwelt﴾ from al-sukna (dwelling), in the sense of tabawwu' (settling) and iṭān (residing). It was used with the preposition fi (in) where it is said: ﴿in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾, following the original usage, because it is transferred from the general sense of sukūn (dwelling), whose proper construction is with bi (in). Or it is from sukūn and lubth (staying), i.e., you settled in their dwellings, at ease, proceeding in their course of wrongdoing, disbelief and sins, not reflecting upon yourselves regarding what befell them, because of what they committed of ruinous deeds. The placing of wronging upon themselves after its general mention earlier is a notice that the calamity of wrongdoing returns to its doer. The meaning of "they" is either all of the nations destroyed before, according to the assumption that the request for respite and the preceding address are specific to the warners, or their first ones, from the people of Noah and Hud, according to the assumption that it is general to all. This address and what follows it are with regard to the condition of their later ones.

﴿And it became clear to you﴾ through witnessing the traces and the successive reports ﴿how We dealt with them﴾ of destruction and punishment for what they did of wrongdoing and corruption. Kayfa (how) is in the accusative by the verb following it, and the clause is not the subject of tabayyana (became clear), as some of the Kufans said; rather its subject is what it clearly indicates, i.e., "We did a strange thing to them." In this there is an emphasis that is not present in saying "what We did to them," as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿surely they will imprison him﴾. It was also read: (wa-bunna).

﴿And We struck for you the parables﴾, i.e., We made clear to you in the Glorious Qur'an, according to the assumption that the address is specific to the warners, or upon the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, according to the assumption that it is general to all wrongdoers, the descriptions of what they did and what was done to them of matters that are strange, like the parables struck for every wrongdoer, so that you may take heed by them, and measure your deeds by their deeds and your end by their end, and move from the descent of the immediate punishment to the descent of the deferred punishment, so that you may refrain from what you were in of disbelief and sins; or We made clear to you that you are like them in disbelief and in deserving punishment. The three clauses are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "you swore," i.e., you swore by eternity, while you had dwelt in the dwellings of those destroyed for their wrongdoing, and it had become clear to you Our strange deed against them, and We warned you about the manifest condition by striking parables. And His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿وَقَدْ مَكَرُوا مَكْرَهُمْ﴾ is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) relating either to the first pronoun in ﴿فَعَلْنا بِهِمْ﴾, or to the second, or to both together. The phrase ﴿وَضَرَبْنا لَكُمُ الأمْثالَ﴾ is placed before it because of its strong connection with what precedes it. The meaning is: We did to them what We did, while they had devised their great scheme against the truth, to nullify it and establish falsehood, a scheme for which they exhausted their effort and went beyond every known limit, to the point that no one other than them could achieve it. The intent is to show how far they went in deserving what was done to them. Alternatively, the meaning is: they had devised the scheme mentioned in arranging the means of survival and in warding off the causes of decline. The purpose is to demonstrate their weakness, the collapse of their power, and its insignificance before the power of God, exalted is He.

﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾ means: the recompense for their scheme that they carried out, whether the word "scheme" is taken as an attribute of its agent, or whether it is understood as God's seizing of them, with "scheme" being attributed to its object. It is called "scheme" either because it corresponds to their scheme in existence and in mention, or because it resembles a scheme in that it comes from a direction they do not perceive. On both interpretations, what is meant is what the words of the Mighty and Majestic ﴿كَيْفَ فَعَلْنا بِهِمْ﴾ convey, and it is not a separate, independent threat. The clause is a *hal* relating to the pronoun in "makaru" (they schemed), meaning: they devised their scheme, while with God is its recompense, or something greater than it. The purpose is to show the corruption of their judgment, in that they engaged in an act while the thing that required its abandonment was clearly present.

﴿وَإنْ كانَ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾ in its magnitude and severity ﴿لِتَزُولَ مِنهُ الجِبالُ﴾ means: even if their scheme was at the utmost degree of firmness and severity. This is expressed by describing it as arranged and prepared, to remove mountains from their places, since it was a parable for that. The clause introduced by *in* of the connective type (*in al-wasliyyah*) is coordinated with an implied clause, and the meaning is: with God is the recompense of their scheme, or the scheme that will befall them, if their scheme was not such that the mountains would be removed by it, even if it was... and so on. That has been omitted by regular elision, because the stated part indicates it clearly. For when a thing is realized in the presence of a strong obstacle, it is all the more realized in its absence. On this point turns the emphasis (*ta'kid ma'nawi*) found in *in al-wasliyyah*, and the apodosis is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, namely the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾. It has been said that *in* is negative and the *lam* is for emphasizing it, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: "وَما كانَ مَكْرُهُمْ" (and their scheme was not...). In that case the clause is a *hal* relating to the pronoun in "makaru", not to the words ﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾, meaning: they devised their scheme, while their scheme was not such that the mountains would be removed by it, where "the mountains" is an expression for the signs of God, His laws, and His miracles manifested through the hands of the earlier messengers, peace be upon them, which are like firm mountains in stability. As for the view that they are an expression for the command of the Prophet ﷺ and the command of the Great Qur'an, as has been said, there is no room for it, since the schemers are the ones who will be destroyed, not those among the addressees who dwelt in their dwellings, even though the address is specifically directed to the warned. It has also been said that *in* is a lightened form of *inna*, and the meaning is: their scheme was indeed such that there would be removed by it what is like mountains in firmness, from the signs, laws, and miracles mentioned. The clause, like the former, is a *hal* relating to the pronoun in "makaru", meaning: they devised their well-known scheme, and the matter was indeed that their scheme was for the removal of the signs and laws, in the sense that it was not valid for such a scheme to come from them, and the nature of the signs and laws prevented them from undertaking a scheme to remove them. Al-Kisa'i read "لَتَزُولُ" with a *fatha* on the *lam*, taking it as the distinguishing *lam* (*al-lam al-farqa*), and the meaning is the magnification of their scheme. The clause is then a *hal* relating to the words ﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾, meaning: with God is the recompense of their scheme, or the scheme against them, while their scheme was such that the mountains would be removed by it, that is, it was of the utmost severity. It was also read with a *fatha* and an accusative ending, according to the dialect of those who put a *fatha* on the *lam* of *kay*. It was also read: "وَإنْ كادَ مَكْرُهُمْ" (even though their scheme nearly...). This is what the noble composition requires and what sound nature inclines towards. It has been said that the pronoun in "makaru" refers to the warned, and what is meant by their scheme is what the words of the Mighty and Majestic convey: ﴿وَإذْ يَمْكُرُ بِكَ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا لِيُثْبِتُوكَ أوْ يَقْتُلُوكَ أوْ يُخْرِجُوكَ﴾ (And when those who disbelieved schemed against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you...), the verse, and other kinds of their scheming against the Messenger of God ﷺ. Perhaps the correct reading in this case is that the words ﴿وَقَدْ مَكَرُوا ...﴾ and so on, are a *hal* relating to the implied speech, meaning: it is said to them what is said, while they, along with what they did of the mentioned oath-taking, together with what contradicts it of dwelling in the dwellings of those who were destroyed, and the clarification of their conditions, and the striking of parables, had devised their great scheme. That is, what came from them was not merely the oath-taking for which they were rebuked, but they dared to commit such a great deed. The words of the Exalted ﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾ are a *hal* relating to the pronoun in "makaru", as we have mentioned before. The words of the Exalted ﴿وَإنْ كانَ مَكْرُهُمْ لِتَزُولَ مِنهُ الجِبالُ﴾ are presented to show that the state does not differ in the realization of the recompense whether their scheme was strong or weak, as has passed there. If *in* is taken as negative, then it is a *hal* relating to the pronoun in "makaru", and the mountains are an expression for the command of the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: they devised, while their scheme was not such that those laws and signs, which are in strength like mountains, would be removed by it. If it is taken as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*, with the *lam* having a *kasra*, it is also a *hal* relating to it, in the sense that that great scheme of theirs was for this purpose, in the sense that it was not valid for such a scheme to come from them, because the matter of the laws is too great for a schemer to scheme against them. If the *lam* has a *fatha*, then it is a *hal* relating to the words ﴿وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ﴾, as we have mentioned before.

فَلْيُتَأمَّلْ:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 14, verse 47:**

﴿So do not think that Allah will break His promise to His messengers.﴾ It is not meant by this, and Allah, glory be to Him, knows best, the promise He made by His saying, ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers﴾ (40:51), and so on. And His saying, ﴿Allah has decreed: "I and My messengers will surely prevail"﴾ (58:21), as has been said, does not restrict it to punishment, especially the punishment of the Hereafter. Rather, it refers to what preceded a little earlier of His promise to punish the wrongdoers, by His saying, ﴿He only defers them﴾ (14:42), and so on. This is made clear by the fa' (the particle "fa'," meaning "so" or "then") that enters upon the prohibition (lā tahsabanna, "do not think"), which is intended to strengthen him, upon him be blessings and peace, in the trust in Allah that he possessed and in his certainty that His promise would be fulfilled. This promise was mentioned together with the command to warn them of the Day when the punishment would come, which includes mention of the punishment of the earlier nations because of their disbelief and their disobedience to their messengers after He had promised them that. Likewise, the story of each of them has been detailed in the Glorious Qur'an. It is as if it were said: Since We have promised you the punishment of the wrongdoers on the Day of Resurrection, and informed you of the hardships they will suffer, and of what they will ask, namely to be returned to the world, and of what We answered them with, and rebuked them for not reflecting on the conditions of those nations before them whom We destroyed for their wrongdoing after We had promised their messengers their destruction, then remain upon the certainty you have held, that We will not break the promise We made to Our messengers. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty﴾, Victorious, who cannot be deceived, and Capable, ﴿Owner of retribution﴾ against His allies' enemies on their behalf. The sentence serves both as a justification (ta'līl) for the aforementioned prohibition and as a concluding remark (tadhyīl) to it. Since the promise was an expression of what we mentioned, namely the punishment of those specific people, the sentence was not concluded by saying, "Indeed, Allah does not break the appointment," but instead it alluded to the attributes of might and retribution, which indicate that. What is meant by retribution is what was indicated by the action, and it was expressed by the term "plotting" (makr).

(p-60) ﴿Yawma tubaddalu al-ardu ghayra al-ardi﴾ is an adverbial of time (*zarf*) governing an implied verb in a new sentence (*mustaʾnif*), to which the prohibition mentioned above extends. That is, "He will carry it out on the day of..." etc. Or it is governed by the preceding clause, as in: "And await the day when the earth will be changed into another earth," or it is for vengeance. It is the same day on which the punishment will come upon them, but it has many aspects, each mentioned under a specific title. Restricting it to this day, although His vengeance extends to all times, is to clarify what is intended by the punishment of the disbelievers delayed until that day, according to the wisdom that calls for it. It was also said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for "the day when the punishment comes to them," or that it is in the accusative governed by "remember" (*udhkur*), or by an implied verb: "He does not break His promise on the day when the earth is changed..." etc. This view also has the same need for justification as the third view. It cannot be in the accusative governed by "breaker of His promise" (*mukhlifa waʿdihi*), because what precedes *inna* (indeed) does not govern what follows it. It was also said that this is not a barrier, because His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed Allah is Mighty, Owner of Retribution" is a parenthetical clause (*jumla iʿtiraḍiyya*), so it is not considered a separating element. Know that change (*tabdil*) may occur in the substance, as in "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars," and His saying, mighty and majestic is He, "We exchanged them for other skins" is of this kind. It may also occur in attributes, as in your saying: "I changed the ring into a seal ring" when you alter its form. From this is His saying: ﴿Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾ according to some views. The noble verse is not explicit in either of the two meanings.

From ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: the earth will be changed into an earth of silver, and the heavens into gold. From Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him: the earth will be changed into another earth, white and pure like silver, in which no blood has been shed and upon which no sin has been committed. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: it is that same earth, but its qualities are changed. He recited:

*"The people are not the people you knew, nor is the abode the abode you used to know."*

The heavens are changed by the scattering of their stars, the eclipsing of their sun, the darkening of their moon, their splitting open, and their becoming gates. This is indicated by what Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, narrated, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth will be changed into another earth, and it will be spread out and stretched like a leather of ʿUkaz; you will not see in it any crookedness or any unevenness."

﴿Wa-l-samawat﴾ means: and the heavens will be changed into other heavens, according to the detail already mentioned. The change of the earth is mentioned first because it is closer to us, and because its change has a greater effect on us.

﴿Wa-barazu﴾ means: the creatures, or the wrongdoers, indicated by the context. The meaning is their emerging from their graves that are in the depths of the earth, or their appearing with their deeds which they used to do secretly and claimed would not be revealed, or doing the deeds of one who claims that. Perhaps attributing the emergence (*buruz*) to them, although it refers to their deeds, is to signal that they will take forms suitable to those deeds. It is coordinated with "will be changed" (*tubaddalu*). The shift to the past tense form (*ṣīgha al-māḍī*) is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence, or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from "the earth," with the implied "qad" (indeed), and the linking element between it and its referent is the *waw*. ﴿Lillahi al-wahidi al-qahhar﴾ means: before Allah, the One, the Subduer, for reckoning and recompense. The mention of the two attributes serves to magnify the gravity of the matter, to inspire awe, to show the invalidity of association with Allah, and to establish vengeance on that day if it is an adverbial of time, and to establish the coming of the promised punishment if it is a substitute for "the day when the punishment comes to them." For when the command belongs to One who is dominant, who is not opposed, and who is powerful, who is not harmed and not outwitted, it is at the utmost degree of severity and difficulty.

﴿And you will see the criminals﴾ is coordinated with ﴿they came forth﴾ ('atf, grammatical coordination). The shift to the present tense (al-'udul ila sighat al-mudari', a shift to the imperfect form) serves either to bring the scene vividly before the listener (istihdar al-surah) or to indicate continuity (al-dalalah 'ala al-istimrar). The coming forth itself, however, is instantaneous (daf'i, occurring at once) and has no continuity to it. If ﴿they came forth﴾ is taken as a circumstantial clause (hal), then ﴿

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 14, verse 50:

﴿Their garments﴾, i.e., their shirts, ﴿of tar﴾. This is a nominal sentence (jumlah min mubtada' wa khabar), whose place is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to "the criminals," or to their pronoun in "muqarranin" (bound together). Its link (rabitah) is the pronoun alone, as in "kallamtuhu fuwahu ila fi" (I spoke to him, his mouth to his mouth). Or it is a resumptive new sentence (musta'nifah). Al-qatiran (tar): that which exudes from the abhal tree (a kind of juniper/tamarisk) and is then boiled, and with which mangy camels are smeared; it burns the mange because of its intense sharpness, and its heat may reach the interior of the body. It is black and foul-smelling, and fire spreads quickly through it. The skins of the people of the Fire are smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like trousers. Thus the four kinds of torment gather upon them: its sting, its burning, the rapid spread of the fire over their skins, and the hideous colour and stench. Yet the disparity between it and what we witness, and between the two kinds of fire, is such that its extent can hardly be measured; it is as though what we witness of them are merely names for their realities in the Hereafter. So by His all-encompassing generosity we seek refuge, and in His vast shelter we take cover.

It is also possible that this is a parable (tamthil) for the vile dispositions surrounding the essence of the soul and its savage defects, which bring upon it pains and griefs. Indeed, it is possible that the aforementioned tar is the very thing they were clothed in during this worldly existence, and which they made their emblem of false beliefs and evil deeds, which attract all kinds of torment. It has become embodied in the Hereafter in that form which entails the intensification of torment. May God, glorified is He, protect us from that by His grace and kindness.

It has been recited as (min qitran), meaning molten copper whose heat has reached its extreme. ﴿And the Fire covers their faces﴾, i.e., it rises above them and surrounds them: the Fire which touches their bodies clothed in tar. The singling out of the faces for the aforementioned judgment, although it generalizes to the rest of their limbs, is because they are the most honoured and noblest of the visible limbs, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Is one who shields his face from the evil of the torment...﴾, and so on. And because they are the gathering place of the senses and faculties which were created for perceiving the truth, and they turned away from it and did not employ them in contemplating it. Just as the heart (fu'ad) is the noblest of the inner organs and the seat of knowledge, and they filled it with ignorances; for this reason it is said: ﴿It rises over the hearts﴾. Or it is because the hearts are free of tar, which makes mention of the fire's covering them unnecessary; perhaps their being left free of it is so that they may recognize one another at moments when the flame is uncovered, and their torment is multiplied with disgrace before the heads of the witnesses.

It has been recited as (taghashsha), meaning "tatagashsha," with one of the two taa' elided. The clause is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, not on the basis that the waw is circumstantial, because it is an affirmative present verb; rather it is on the basis that it is conjoined to the circumstance (al-hal). So said Abu al-Baqa'.

The phrase ﴿So that Allah may recompense﴾ is related to an implied verb (*mudmar*, an omitted element). The meaning is: He does this to them so that He may recompense ﴿every soul﴾ that committed crimes ﴿for what it has earned﴾ of kinds of disbelief and sins, with a recompense corresponding to its deeds. In this there is an indication that their recompense is proportionate to their deeds. Or it is related to His words "﴿they came forth﴾" (*barazu*), on the assumption that it is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) with "﴿is changed﴾" (*tubaddalu*), and the pronoun refers to the creation. His words "And you see the criminals..." etc. are a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) between the linked element (*mutaʿallaq*) and that to which it is linked (*mutaʿallaq bihi*). That is: they came forth for the reckoning, so that Allah may recompense every soul, whether obedient or disobedient, for what it has earned of good or evil. The mention of the punishment of the disobedient has been sufficient, relying on the testimony of the context, especially in view of the precedence of the all-encompassing mercy.

﴿Indeed, Allah is swift in reckoning﴾, since no matter preoccupies Him from another, so He completes it in the briefest of time, and so He fulfils the recompense in accordance with what is due. Or: He is swift in coming, He will come soon. Or: He is swift in retribution, as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿and He is swift in reckoning﴾.

**This** refers to what has been mentioned from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And do not think that Allah is unaware﴾ up to ﴿swift in reckoning﴾.

﴿A message﴾: a sufficiency in admonition and reminder without need for what this noble surah contains, or all of the glorious Qur'an contains of the kinds of admonitions and calamities, ﴿for mankind﴾, specifically for the disbelievers, on the reckoning that the warning is restricted to them in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And warn mankind﴾; or for them and for the believers in general, on the reckoning that it also includes them, even though what has been explained is specific to the wrongdoers.

﴿And that they may be warned thereby﴾: this is conjoined to an implied element. The lam is connected to "a message": that is, a sufficiency for them so that they may give heed and be warned by it; or "this is a message for them, so that they may understand it, and that they may be warned by it," on the reckoning that "message" means "conveyance," as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿The Messenger's duty is only conveyance﴾. Or it is connected to an implied element: that is, "and that they may be warned by it, which was sent down" or "which was recited." It was also read as "liyanzarū bihi" (*liyanthurū*), from "nadhira al-shay'," when one knows a thing, beware of it and prepares for it.

﴿And that they may know﴾ by reflecting on what it contains of clear proofs, which are the destruction of nations and the settling of others in their dwellings, and other things that came before and after, ﴿that He is only one God﴾, with no partner. The warning is placed first because it is what calls to reflection, which leads to what is its goal from the aforementioned knowledge. The reminder in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And that those of understanding may take heed﴾, means: that they may remember what they used to do before of monotheism and other matters of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and His dealings with His servants, so that they may refrain from what would ruin them of the attributes with which the disbelievers are characterized, and fortify themselves with what would win them favor of sound beliefs and righteous deeds. In specifying the reminder for those of understanding there is an allusion that knowledge is specific to the disbelievers, and an indication that what is referred to by "this" is what we have mentioned of the calamities directed toward their situation, not the whole surah that contains them, and also what preceded for the believers as well, for in it there is what gives them a new benefit. Since what the message conveys of monotheism, and what follows from it of rulings in relation to the disbelievers, is a new matter, and in relation to those of understanding is steadfastness upon that, as indicated, he expressed the first by "knowledge," and the second by "reminder." The order of existence was observed, together with what it contains of ending with the good, and Allah, glorified is He, knows best. May Allah end for us with happiness and the good, and grant us success in gaining His pleasure in this world and the Hereafter. Amen.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Ibrahim will be given ten good deeds for each number of those who worshipped idols and those who did not worship them."

And praise belongs to Allah alone.
